domains.name: Group Work & Collaboration
domains.summary: Group projects, assessed group presentations and collaborative reports are common across disciplines, yet students often receive little guidance on how to collaborate, and multilingual students can be positioned as less competent and allocated marginal roles. This domain covers why universities assess collaboration and how groups plan and allocate work, run meetings, negotiate disagreement, write together, and document and evaluate contributions. It treats equitable participation as a shared responsibility of all group members and of course design, not as a deficit of particular students.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to plan and organise group projects, run useful meetings, deal with disagreement, write together and show what you and others contributed, while making sure everyone in a multilingual group can take a full part.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce the purposes of group work, simple role allocation and meeting routines through scaffolded projects with explicit ground rules and teacher monitoring.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Use short group projects to practise planning, meeting language and inclusive participation among students from varied backgrounds, in preparation for assessed group work on degree programmes.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support assessed group projects with meeting management, conflict handling, collaborative writing workflows and peer evaluation of contributions.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Address intensive, often highly multilingual group assignments in which students must quickly establish roles, resolve disagreements and document contributions for peer-moderated marks.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on research-team meetings, co-authoring and documenting contributions, linking collaboration to authorship norms and professional conduct.

domains.name: Presentations
domains.summary: Academic presentations range from short assessed talks on foundation and pre-sessional programmes to conference papers, posters and research seminars at doctoral level. This domain treats the presentation as a spoken, multimodal genre designed for listeners who process information once, in real time: it needs explicit structure and signposting, visuals that support rather than duplicate speech, intelligible prosody and a delivery mode between reading a script and improvising. It gives particular attention to the interactive phases — openings and question-and-answer sessions — which research on conference presentations shows are central to how presenters engage audiences and establish credibility.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to plan, design and deliver academic presentations that listeners can follow, how to talk an audience through visuals and data, and how to handle questions, from short class talks to posters and research presentations.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build clear structure, signposting, delivery from notes and basic slide design through short, rehearsed presentations, often in groups, on accessible topics.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Develop individual presentations on a researched topic that use sources and data and include timed questions, often as part of progression assessment.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support module-specific presentation tasks, including group presentations and recorded assessments, with attention to disciplinary expectations and audience.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on presenting projects and dissertation plans, explaining data, handling challenging questions and working in recorded or online formats.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address research seminars, conference papers, posters and upgrade or progression presentations within strict time limits, framing contribution for specialist audiences and engaging productively in discussion sessions.

domains.name: Seminars & Discussion
domains.summary: Seminars, tutorials and discussion groups are where students are expected to co-construct understanding of readings and ideas in real time, and where participation is often assessed formally or informally. This domain treats discussion as negotiated, multi-turn interaction rather than a list of functional phrases: learners need to prepare substantively, find and hold turns, state and justify positions, mitigate disagreement, build on and summarise others' contributions and, at higher levels, facilitate. Participation is also shaped by anxiety, positioning and the way tutors and peers distribute the floor, so the domain addresses willingness to communicate and the conditions for participation, not only individual skill.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how university discussions work and how to prepare for them, get into the conversation, make and support your points, respond to others politely but critically, and help a discussion move forward, face to face or online.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Make seminar purposes and participation expectations explicit, and build reliable resources for giving views, asking questions and checking understanding through short, well-prepared, low-stakes discussions on accessible content.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Move from rehearsed phrases to extended negotiation of ideas from set readings, with explicit work on turn-taking, mitigated disagreement and referring to sources, often in an assessed seminar that informs progression.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed practice in learners' own modules, focusing on subject-specific expectations, entering fast discussions with peers who share local references, and building on others' points.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise critical engagement with readings, citing in speech, facilitating and summarising in intensive one-year programmes where seminar contribution may be assessed from the first weeks.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on research group meetings, reading groups and peer seminars on work in progress, where researchers question, critique and are questioned as emerging members of a discipline.

topics.name: Purposes of group work
topics.description: Explain why universities use group work and assessed collaboration — for example to develop teamwork, to tackle tasks too large for individuals and to bring together diverse perspectives — and identify what a given task assesses: the product, the process, individual contributions or a combination. Understanding purposes and assessment design helps learners set realistic expectations and treat group tasks as collaborative learning rather than as work to be divided and stapled together.
masteryEvidence: Identifies from an assessment brief what is assessed (product, process, individual contribution) and how marks are allocated
Explains at least two learning purposes of group work in their discipline
Distinguishes cooperative division of labour from collaborative joint construction and says which a given task requires
Locates the rules on permitted collaboration and on any individually assessed components of the task
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a group assignment brief and ask: 'What exactly will be marked, how will individual marks be decided, and what will you need to do together rather than separately?' Look for an accurate reading of mark allocation and individual components; a gap response assumes everyone receives the same mark for combining separately written sections.

topics.name: Roles and planning
topics.description: Plan a group project by analysing the task, agreeing ground rules (communication channels, response times, decision-making, quality standards), allocating roles and tasks on the basis of expertise and development goals, and setting milestones with internal deadlines, recorded in a shared place. Explicit early planning reduces later conflict and helps ensure that every member, including multilingual members, has a defined and substantive role.
masteryEvidence: Contributes to a written ground-rules agreement covering communication, decision-making and deadlines
Proposes a task breakdown derived from the assignment brief and criteria
Negotiates a role allocation that balances expertise with development and does not confine any member to peripheral tasks
Sets milestones with internal deadlines well before the submission date
Records the plan in a shared, accessible location and refers back to it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a group 20 minutes and an assignment brief to produce a one-page plan, and observe the discussion. Check for ground rules, a task breakdown linked to the brief, roles negotiated with all members and dated milestones; a gap is a plan that divides the word count equally with no internal deadlines and roles assigned without discussion.

topics.name: Running group meetings
topics.description: Run and take part in group meetings by preparing and circulating an agenda, chairing or timekeeping, reaching and recording decisions, and producing brief minutes with action points, owners and deadlines that are followed up at the next meeting. Well-structured meetings make decisions and responsibilities visible and accountable, which matters when contributions are later assessed.
masteryEvidence: Drafts a short agenda with items, purposes and time allocations
Chairs an item by stating its purpose, inviting views and moving the group to a decision
Uses language to propose, test for consensus and confirm decisions
Writes minutes that record decisions and action points with owners and deadlines rather than narrating the discussion
Reviews action points at the start of the next meeting
topics.assessmentPrompt: Observe a 15-minute simulated project meeting chaired by the learner and collect their minutes. Check for an agenda, time management, explicit decisions and action points with owners and dates; a gap is a discussion that ends without a recorded decision, or minutes that narrate the conversation.

topics.name: Managing disagreement and conflict
topics.description: Manage disagreement and conflict in group work by distinguishing disagreements about ideas from problems of process or contribution, raising concerns early and specifically with reference to agreed ground rules, negotiating solutions, and escalating to tutors through appropriate channels with evidence when internal resolution fails. Unaddressed problems tend to surface late, when options are limited.
masteryEvidence: Raises a process or contribution concern early and specifically, referring to the agreed ground rules
Describes the problem's impact and proposes a solution in mitigated but unambiguous language
Distinguishes a productive disagreement about ideas from interpersonal or process conflict and responds accordingly
Negotiates a compromise or an agreed decision rule when the group is divided
Documents unresolved issues and escalates to the module team with evidence when internal resolution fails
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present a scenario in which one member has missed two internal deadlines. Ask the learner to role-play raising this in a meeting, then to draft a short message to the tutor in case it continues. Check for specificity, reference to ground rules, a proposed solution and proportionate escalation; a gap is either avoidance or an accusatory message without evidence.

topics.name: Inclusive collaboration in multilingual groups
topics.description: Collaborate equitably in multilingual groups by accommodating to varied accents and proficiency levels, creating space for all members to contribute substantively, drawing on members' different linguistic, disciplinary and educational backgrounds, and challenging exclusionary patterns such as allocating tasks by assumed language ability. Equitable participation is a responsibility of every member, including the most proficient users of English, and supports the quality of the group's work.
masteryEvidence: Adjusts their own speech (pace, idiom, local references, checking) to support mutual intelligibility in the group
Invites and builds on contributions from members who speak less
Proposes participation structures that widen participation (e.g. rounds, written input before discussion, rotating roles)
Notices and tactfully raises it when a member's ideas are overlooked or their role is marginalised
Draws on members' different backgrounds as resources for the task
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show a 3-minute recording or transcript of a multilingual group meeting in which one member's suggestion is ignored and roles are allocated by assumed language ability. Ask the learner what they notice and what they would do. Strong: identifies the exclusion and proposes concrete moves; partial: notices the issue but frames it as that member's language problem; gap: notices nothing.

topics.name: Collaborative writing
topics.description: Co-author a group report or document by agreeing a structure and style sheet, using shared documents with comments, suggestion mode and version history, integrating sections into a coherent whole with consistent terminology, voice and referencing, and revising the whole text together. Collaborative writing requires coordination of text, not only division of labour, and must respect the boundary between group work and individually assessed components.
masteryEvidence: Agrees with co-authors a structure, a style sheet (terminology, tense, citation style) and an editing workflow
Uses comments, suggestion mode and version history to propose and track changes respectfully
Writes transitions and cross-references that integrate their section with others'
Edits a combined draft for consistency of terminology, voice and referencing
Distinguishes legitimate co-authoring from individually assessed components, following the brief
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two sections of a group report written by different students, with inconsistent terminology and citation format and no link between them. Ask them to identify the problems and propose a revision workflow. Check whether they spot terminology, voice and referencing inconsistencies and propose a shared style sheet and an integrating edit; a gap response proposes proofreading only.

topics.name: Assessing contributions
topics.description: Evaluate one's own and peers' contributions to group work against agreed criteria, document one's own role with evidence (minutes, version history, task logs), and describe contributions accurately in peer-evaluation forms and individual reflections. Peer evaluation can affect individual marks and can reproduce biases, for example equating fluent talk with contribution, so criterion-referenced, evidenced judgement matters.
masteryEvidence: Rates contributions against stated criteria rather than general impressions or friendship
Supports ratings with specific evidence such as minutes, version history or completed tasks
Describes their own contribution accurately in a reflection, including its limitations
Credits less visible contributions (research, editing, coordination) as well as visible ones
Distinguishes a member's spoken fluency from the quality and quantity of their contribution
topics.assessmentPrompt: Provide a short project log and minutes showing who did what, and ask the learner to complete a peer-evaluation form for two members with a one-sentence justification for each rating. Check whether ratings are criterion-based and evidenced and whether less visible work is credited; a gap is equal ratings with no evidence, or ratings driven by who spoke most in meetings.

topics.name: Purpose and audience analysis
topics.description: Analyse the purpose of a presentation (to inform, explain, persuade, report research or propose) and the audience's prior knowledge, expectations and relationship to the speaker, and adapt content selection, technical density, register and interaction accordingly. Audience analysis drives later decisions about structure, visuals and delivery, and is what distinguishes a presentation from a reading of an essay.
masteryEvidence: States the purpose of a planned presentation and what the audience should know or do afterwards in one or two sentences
Identifies what the audience already knows and decides which terms to define and which background to omit
Produces specialist and non-specialist versions of the same talk that differ in content, terminology and examples, not only in formality
Selects content to fit the time and audience rather than including everything they know
Anticipates likely audience questions or objections at the planning stage
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short abstract and ask them to outline how a 5-minute talk on it would differ for (a) classmates from another discipline and (b) the module tutor. Look for changes in terminology, background, examples and purpose; a gap response changes only greetings and formality markers while keeping identical content.

topics.name: Structuring a presentation
topics.description: Organise a presentation into an introduction, body and conclusion with an explicit roadmap, a limited number of main points, internal summaries and a conclusion that returns to the purpose, designed for listeners who cannot re-read. Spoken structure needs more redundancy and explicit signalling than written text, so an essay cannot simply be read or summarised section by section.
masteryEvidence: Produces a plan with a stated purpose, three or four main points and a conclusion that returns to the purpose
Includes a roadmap that matches the actual order of the talk
Provides an internal summary or bridging transition at the end of each main section
Allocates time across sections in proportion to their importance
Restructures a written essay or report into a presentation plan rather than following it paragraph by paragraph
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 600-word essay and 15 minutes to produce a 5-minute presentation outline from it. Check for a purpose statement, fewer main points than the essay, a roadmap, transitions and a conclusion; a gap outline mirrors the essay paragraph by paragraph with no roadmap or internal summaries.

topics.name: Opening a presentation
topics.description: Open a presentation by establishing context and relevance, engaging the audience, stating the purpose or central claim and previewing the structure, selecting and ordering these moves to suit the audience and genre. The opening sets the audience's interpretive frame and the speaker's credibility, and research on conference introductions shows that interpersonal engagement matters here as much as content.
masteryEvidence: Establishes why the topic matters to this audience within the first minute
States the purpose or central claim explicitly
Previews the structure in a way consistent with the rest of the talk
Uses at least one engagement move suited to the context (e.g. a shared reference point, a question to the audience, inclusive 'we', a brief relevant case)
Avoids lengthy self-introduction or apology that delays the purpose
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to deliver only the first 60–90 seconds of a planned presentation. Check for context and relevance, purpose, a preview and an engagement move, and whether a listener could predict the structure from it; a gap opening is a title read aloud followed by an apology, or immediate detail with no stated purpose.

topics.name: Signposting in presentations
topics.description: Use spoken signposting to announce structure, mark transitions, highlight key points, summarise and conclude, combining lexical markers with prosodic signals such as pausing and pitch reset at boundaries. Signposting helps listeners build a mental map of the talk, but its density should match the length and audience of the talk, since mechanical or excessive markers distract.
masteryEvidence: Uses macro-markers to announce the overall structure and each major transition
Marks key points with relevance markers supported by prosodic emphasis
Gives brief internal summaries before moving to a new section
Pauses and resets pitch at section boundaries
Varies signposting language and adjusts its density to the talk's length and audience
topics.assessmentPrompt: Record a 3-minute section of the learner's talk and ask a listener to sketch its structure from the audio alone; compare the sketch with the learner's plan. Strong: the sketch matches, with transitions marked lexically and prosodically; partial: lexical markers are present but delivered without pausing, so boundaries blur; gap: the listener cannot reconstruct the sections.

topics.name: Designing slides
topics.description: Design slides and other visual aids that support the spoken message: one main point per slide, headings that state that point, minimal text, readable type, purposeful and simplified figures, clear visual hierarchy, accessible colour and contrast, and attribution of images and data. Slides should complement speech rather than duplicate it, because dense slide text competes with the speaker for the audience's attention.
masteryEvidence: Writes slide headings that state the point of the slide rather than a topic label
Reduces slide text to phrases, key terms and data that support rather than duplicate what is said
Selects and simplifies figures so that the feature being discussed is visible and legible at a distance
Applies accessible design: sufficient contrast, readable font size, and meaning not carried by colour alone
Attributes images, figures and data sources on the slide
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a text-heavy slide containing a complex chart copied from a paper and five minutes to redesign it. Check for a heading that states the point, reduced text, a simplified or highlighted chart, accessible contrast and source attribution; a gap redesign changes colours or fonts but keeps full sentences and the unsimplified chart.

topics.name: Talking about visuals and data
topics.description: Guide an audience through a chart, table or diagram by orienting them to what it shows (type, axes, units, categories), highlighting the one to three features that matter, and stating their significance for the argument, while synchronising speech with pointing or slide builds. Audiences cannot study a visual at their own pace, so the presenter must direct attention selectively.
masteryEvidence: Orients the audience to the visual's type, variables and units before interpreting it
Highlights one to three significant features rather than describing every data point
States what the highlighted pattern means for the point being made
Synchronises spoken reference with gesture, pointer or animation so the audience looks at the right place
Says numbers, ranges and units aloud accurately and approximates where precision is unnecessary
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner an unfamiliar bar or line chart for one minute, then ask them to explain it to the group in 60 seconds. Check for orientation, selective highlighting, interpretation and accurate number expressions; a gap response reads out values from left to right with no interpretation.

topics.name: Vocal delivery
topics.description: Control pace, volume, pausing, thought groups, prominence and intonation so that a presentation is intelligible and easy to follow, prioritising the prosodic features that most affect listeners' understanding over accent reduction. Prosody signals structure, new and contrastive information, and the speaker's engagement with the audience.
masteryEvidence: Divides speech into thought groups with pauses at meaningful boundaries
Places prominence on new and contrastive information, including correct stress in key technical terms
Maintains a pace and volume the audience can follow, slowing for key points and numbers
Uses intonation to signal continuation, completion and engagement rather than a level monotone
Evaluates a recording of their own delivery against prioritised intelligibility features and sets a specific target
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to read aloud an unmarked 100-word excerpt from their own script after one minute's preparation, then deliver the same content from notes. Check pause placement, prominence on key words and pace in both; a gap response shows evenly spaced pauses unrelated to meaning, prominence on function words, or a rate that rises under pressure.

topics.name: Non-verbal communication
topics.description: Use gaze, facial expression, gesture, posture and position in the room to support the spoken message, direct attention to visuals and connect with the audience, adapting to the setting and to one's own physical and neurological needs. Non-verbal norms vary across contexts and individuals, so the aim is purposeful, non-distracting use rather than conformity to a single model of 'confident' body language.
masteryEvidence: Distributes gaze across the audience rather than fixing it on notes, the screen or one person
Uses gesture to point to visuals and to mark structure or emphasis
Positions themselves so as not to block the screen and faces the audience when speaking about slides
Reduces distracting habits identified through video self-review
Adapts non-verbal behaviour for online or recorded formats (camera framing, looking at the lens)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Video the learner presenting for two minutes and review it together with the sound off, asking them to identify what helps and what distracts. Check whether gaze is distributed, gestures are linked to content and position supports the visuals; a gap is sustained reading from the screen with the back to the audience.

topics.name: Speaking from notes
topics.description: Deliver a presentation from brief prompts (key words, cue cards, slide notes) rather than reading a full script or reciting a memorised text, using the notes to retrieve structure and key wording while formulating sentences in the moment, and scripting only selected high-risk segments. Read-aloud written prose is lexically dense and usually prosodically flat, which makes it hard for listeners to process.
masteryEvidence: Reduces a full script to key-word prompts that show structure, key terms, numbers and transitions
Delivers a section from prompts using spoken-style, clause-based sentences rather than written-style ones
Scripts and memorises only selected high-risk parts (opening line, key definitions, transitions)
Looks up from notes for most of the delivery
Recovers when losing their place by moving to the next prompt
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to convert one paragraph of their script into no more than ten prompt words and then deliver it from the prompts. Compare the delivery with the script: strong delivery uses shorter, clause-based spoken sentences with eye contact; partial delivery is near-verbatim recall with long pauses; a gap is reading the script.

topics.name: Handling questions
topics.description: Manage question-and-answer sessions by listening to the whole question, clarifying or reformulating it, answering concisely and relevantly, acknowledging limits honestly, and deferring or redirecting when appropriate, including when the turn is a critical comment rather than a question. Q&A is the least predictable part of a presentation and a key site for demonstrating understanding and establishing credibility.
masteryEvidence: Confirms or reformulates a question before answering when it is long, unclear or critical
Answers concisely, linking back to the presentation's content or evidence
Acknowledges a limitation or gap in knowledge honestly, with a hedge or an offer to follow up
Responds to a critical comment by acknowledging it and then clarifying or defending, without defensiveness
Manages time and multiple questioners fairly
topics.assessmentPrompt: After a short presentation, ask three prepared questions: a clarification question, a challenge to the evidence, and a question outside the presenter's scope. Check for reformulation, concision, honest acknowledgement of limits and composure; a gap response answers a different question from the one asked, over-elaborates, or says 'I don't know' with no acknowledgement or offer.

topics.name: Group presentations
topics.description: Plan and deliver a presentation as a group by agreeing a single message and structure, allocating sections by content rather than by person, making handovers that link sections, keeping slides, terminology and referencing consistent, and sharing the Q&A. Assessed group presentations test coordination as well as individual delivery, and a poorly integrated talk often reveals divided rather than shared planning.
masteryEvidence: Agrees with the group a single purpose and overall structure before sections are divided
Delivers handovers that summarise their section and introduce the next speaker's point
Refers to other members' sections to build cohesion across speakers
Uses a consistent slide template, terminology and citation style with the rest of the group
Shares the Q&A by directing questions to the most appropriate member and supporting each other's answers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Watch a group run-through and ask each member to state the presentation's overall message in one sentence. Check consistency across members, the quality of handovers and whether sections refer to one another; a gap is four mini-presentations with different messages and handovers limited to names ('Now X will talk').

topics.name: Poster presentations
topics.description: Present an academic poster by preparing short and longer spoken overviews, gauging each visitor's background and interest, guiding them through the poster's reading path, and sustaining a one-to-one or small-group discussion that includes questions, critique and follow-up. Poster sessions are interactive and conversational, and much of a poster's value lies in the conversations it supports.
masteryEvidence: Delivers a 1–2-minute overview that states the research question, approach, key finding and implication
Adjusts the depth of explanation after gauging the visitor's background
Points visitors to the relevant section or figure while explaining
Invites visitors to connect the work to their own interests or research
Handles critical questions and records useful feedback or contacts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Run a mock poster session in which the learner meets two visitors with contrasting backgrounds (a specialist and a non-specialist). Check the overview's length and content, adaptation to each visitor, use of the poster to guide attention and handling of questions; a gap is the same memorised speech delivered to both visitors regardless of their responses.

topics.name: Research and conference presentations
topics.description: Present research to specialist audiences in conference papers, research seminars and dissertation or progression presentations, framing the niche and contribution early, selecting findings and visuals that carry a clear take-home message, keeping to strict time limits and engaging with the discussion session. These presentations socialise researchers into disciplinary communities, and their introductions and discussion phases are particularly consequential for credibility.
masteryEvidence: Frames the research gap and contribution explicitly within the first minutes for a specialist audience
Selects a subset of findings and visuals that support a clear take-home message within the time limit
Presents methods at a level of detail that allows evaluation without overwhelming the argument
Keeps to time by cutting content in advance rather than rushing at the end
Treats discussion-session comments as contributions to the research and notes follow-up actions
Adapts the talk to the format (e.g. short conference slot, long research seminar, work-in-progress peer seminar)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to deliver the first three minutes and the final minute of a conference-length talk on their research, followed by two questions. Check whether the niche and contribution are clear by minute three, whether the conclusion states a take-home message, and whether answers engage with questions as dialogue; a gap is extended background with no clear contribution, followed by a rushed list of all results.

topics.name: Recorded and online presentations
topics.description: Produce recorded and live online presentations by planning for microphone, camera and screen-sharing, maintaining spoken-style delivery and audience engagement without live feedback, editing within the assessment's rules, and providing accurate captions or transcripts. Recorded formats invite scripting and repeated re-recording, so learners need to manage naturalness, authenticity and compliance with task regulations.
masteryEvidence: Sets up audio, lighting and framing so that speech is clear and the speaker visible
Coordinates screen-sharing or slide recording with spoken explanation without long silences
Maintains spoken-style delivery from prompts rather than reading a visible script
Follows assessment rules on editing, length, file format and the use of AI or third-party tools
Provides captions or a transcript and corrects automatic captions for technical terms and names
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to submit a 2-minute recorded section of a presentation with a short note on how it was produced. Check audio clarity, synchronisation with slides, spoken-style delivery, caption accuracy for technical terms and compliance with the task rules; a gap is a voice-over read from a dense script with uncorrected automatic captions.

topics.name: Rehearsal and timing
topics.description: Rehearse a presentation aloud, with timing and under realistic conditions, using recordings and peer feedback to refine content, transitions and delivery, and adjust content in advance so that it fits the time limit. Rehearsal reduces the planning and formulation load of live delivery and is the main safeguard against overrunning.
masteryEvidence: Rehearses aloud at least twice with timing, a recording or a live listener
Identifies sections that overrun and cuts or condenses them before delivery, not during it
Plans section-by-section time checkpoints and monitors progress against them
Uses rehearsal feedback to revise transitions and difficult phrases
Prepares a shortened version for when the available time is reduced
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to report planned and actual rehearsal timings for each section and what they changed as a result. Strong: specific checkpoints and evidence of cuts made in advance; partial: rehearsed silently or only the first half; gap: no rehearsal aloud and a plan to speak faster if time runs short.

topics.name: Purposes and expectations of seminars
topics.description: Explain what seminars, tutorials and discussion classes are for in a given programme — co-constructing understanding of readings and concepts, testing ideas and showing engagement — and how participation is expected, and sometimes assessed. Because these expectations are largely tacit and vary by discipline, level, class size and tutor, knowing them helps learners interpret silence, interruption and critique and decide how to contribute.
masteryEvidence: Describes the purposes of at least two discussion formats in their programme (e.g. tutorial, reading seminar, problem class) and what counts as a useful contribution in each
Distinguishes a seminar from a lecture in terms of who is expected to speak, what preparation is assumed and how ideas are developed
Identifies from a module handbook or assessment criteria whether and how participation is assessed
Explains why tentative, partial or questioning contributions can be valued, not only 'correct answers'
Describes differences in participation norms observed between tutors, modules or disciplines
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner a short module description with a participation criterion and ask: 'What would a good contribution in this seminar look like, and what would the tutor expect you to have done beforehand?' Look for reference to preparation, developing readings and peers' ideas, and recognition that questions and partial ideas count; a gap response equates participation with answering the tutor's questions correctly.

topics.name: Preparing for seminars
topics.description: Prepare for a seminar by reading the set texts with the discussion questions in mind, noting key claims with page references, reactions and points of uncertainty, and planning two or three possible contributions and questions in note form. Preparation reduces real-time processing load so that learners can attend to the discussion and enter it with substantive content rather than summary.
masteryEvidence: Brings notes on each set reading recording the main claim, one piece of evidence and a page or section reference
Prepares at least two contributions phrased as positions or as connections between readings, not only summaries
Formulates at least one genuine question about a point of difficulty or disagreement in the reading
Anticipates likely discussion questions from the module outline or tutor prompts and plans brief note-form responses
Checks the meaning and pronunciation of key terms so that they can be used fluently in discussion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before a seminar, ask the learner to show their preparation notes for one reading and say what they plan to contribute. Check whether the notes go beyond summary to include a position, a link to another text or session, and a question, with page references; a gap response is a highlighted text with no notes, or a full paragraph scripted to read aloud.

topics.name: Turn-taking and taking the floor
topics.description: Enter, hold and yield turns in multi-party academic discussion by recognising likely transition points, using brief floor-claiming and floor-holding moves, and judging when overlap or interruption is acceptable in a particular group. Because turns in student discussion are often taken by self-selection rather than allocated by the tutor, learners who wait to be invited may have few opportunities to contribute.
masteryEvidence: Enters a discussion at a transition point with a short bridging move that links to the previous speaker before making their point
Holds the floor while formulating, using fillers or announced structure, rather than falling silent mid-turn
Yields the turn explicitly by inviting a response or passing to a named participant
Re-enters after a failed attempt or overlap at the next opportunity
Adjusts the frequency and length of their turns to the group, avoiding both prolonged silence and domination
topics.assessmentPrompt: Record a 10-minute student-led discussion of four to six participants and tally, for the learner, self-selected entries, invited entries, failed attempts and turn length; then ask them to explain one moment when they wanted to speak but did not. Strong learners self-select at transition points with linking moves and can name the cues they used; partial learners speak mainly when invited; a gap is near-silence or long, unlinked monologues.

topics.name: Expressing and justifying views
topics.description: State a position on a question or reading clearly and support it with reasons, examples or evidence, using language for stating positions, giving reasons and exemplifying, and signalling how firmly the view is held. In seminars both unsupported assertion and unpositioned summary are weak contributions; a short claim–reason–support move that can be extended under questioning is the basic unit of contribution.
masteryEvidence: States a position in one clear sentence before elaborating it
Supports the position with at least one reason and one example or piece of evidence
Signals the strength of the view (tentative, qualified or firm) in a way that matches the support offered
Distinguishes their own view from a summary of the reading when speaking
Responds to 'Why?' or 'What's the evidence?' by extending the reasoning rather than repeating the claim
topics.assessmentPrompt: Pose a contestable question about a familiar reading, allow one minute's planning, and ask for a 45-second contribution; then ask 'Why do you think that?' Look for a stated position, a reason and support, and a second response that adds a new reason or qualification; a gap response summarises the reading without taking a position, or repeats the claim when challenged.

topics.name: Agreeing and disagreeing
topics.description: Agree, partially agree and disagree with peers, tutors and authors in ways that make the point of difference explicit while maintaining collegial relationships, typically by acknowledging the other position, locating the specific difference and giving a reason, with mitigation adjusted to the relationship and the stakes. Seminars value disagreement about ideas, but bald disagreement can damage relationships and over-hedged disagreement can obscure the speaker's position.
masteryEvidence: Disagrees by acknowledging the previous point, stating the specific point of difference and giving a reason
Uses partial agreement to accept one aspect of a claim while challenging another
Adjusts the degree of mitigation to the interlocutor's role and the seriousness of the disagreement
Disagrees with a tutor or a published author without either deferring entirely or sounding dismissive
Responds to disagreement with their own view by clarifying, conceding or defending rather than withdrawing from the exchange
topics.assessmentPrompt: Read or play a 30-second contribution containing a debatable claim about a familiar reading and ask the learner to respond as if in a seminar where they partly disagree. Check for acknowledgement, a precisely located difference, a reason and mitigation proportionate to the context; a gap response is either a bare 'I disagree' with no reason or so much hedging that the listener cannot tell what the learner thinks.

topics.name: Building on others' contributions
topics.description: Link a contribution explicitly to what others have said by extending, qualifying, exemplifying, connecting or contrasting their points, and attribute those points to the speaker. Building on others is how ideas are co-constructed across turns in seminars, and it makes listening visible as well as thinking.
masteryEvidence: Begins contributions with an explicit link to a named peer's point and states the relation (extend, qualify, contrast, exemplify)
Reformulates a peer's point accurately before developing it
Connects two earlier contributions that the group has not yet related to each other
Adds an example, counter-example or source that develops another speaker's idea
Credits peers' ideas when reusing them later in the discussion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Choose three of the learner's turns from a recorded discussion and ask them what each turn was responding to and how. Strong: each turn is explicitly linked to a specific prior contribution and develops its content; partial: links are generic ('Following on from that…') without engaging the content; gap: turns are pre-prepared points unrelated to the preceding talk.

topics.name: Asking questions and seeking clarification
topics.description: Formulate questions that seek clarification, elaboration, evidence or implications from tutors and peers, pinpointing which term, claim or step the question concerns and choosing direct or mitigated forms suited to the relationship. Asking questions is both a comprehension-repair strategy and a legitimate form of contribution, and subject lecturers have identified it as an oral demand that multilingual students can find difficult.
masteryEvidence: Asks a clarification question that pinpoints the specific term, claim or step not understood
Asks for elaboration, evidence or implications in a way that invites a developed answer
Produces well-formed direct and indirect (embedded) questions
Mitigates questions to tutors appropriately without obscuring what is being asked
Asks at least one question that opens further discussion rather than one answerable with a single fact
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a 2-minute recorded talk extract containing one ambiguous term and one unsupported claim, and ask the learner to put two questions to the speaker as if present. Check that one question pinpoints the ambiguity and one asks for support or elaboration, with suitable mitigation and intelligible form; a gap response is a generic 'Can you repeat?' or 'I don't understand.'

topics.name: Checking and confirming understanding
topics.description: Confirm mutual understanding during discussion by paraphrasing others' points for confirmation, checking that one's own point has been understood, and reformulating it with simpler wording, an example or a definition when it has not. In multilingual groups whose members differ in accent, proficiency and disciplinary background, explicit confirmation and reformulation are routine collaborative moves rather than signs of weakness.
masteryEvidence: Paraphrases a peer's point and asks for confirmation before responding to it
Notices signs that their own point has not been understood and reformulates it with different wording or an example
Uses confirmation checks at a frequency that supports rather than interrupts the discussion
Glosses a technical term or acronym for listeners from other disciplines when first using it
Distinguishes a misunderstanding of language from a disagreement about content and responds accordingly
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a pair task, give each learner a different short text to explain; the listener must paraphrase back before responding and is privately instructed to misunderstand once. Observe whether the learner checks understanding, paraphrases accurately and repairs their explanation when the partner's paraphrase is wrong; a gap is repeating the same words more loudly.

topics.name: Referring to readings and evidence in discussion
topics.description: Refer to set readings, data and other sources in discussion with brief spoken attribution (author or text, the relevant point and, where useful, a page or section), keeping the source's claim distinct from one's own interpretation. Oral attribution makes contributions checkable, shows engagement with the reading and lets peers locate the passage under discussion.
masteryEvidence: Attributes a point to a specific reading with a spoken signal phrase and, where helpful, a page or section reference
Marks the boundary between what the source says and their own evaluation of it
Paraphrases briefly instead of reading long quotations aloud
Uses a source to support, qualify or challenge a peer's point
Reports a source's stance with an appropriate reporting verb (e.g. argues, suggests, finds)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to make a 1-minute seminar contribution that uses one set reading to support or challenge a view. Check for clear attribution, a brief and accurate paraphrase, a locator where useful and an audible boundary between source and own comment; a gap response is an unattributed claim, or a long read-aloud quotation with no comment.

topics.name: Facilitating discussion
topics.description: Lead or chair a discussion by framing the task with an open question, inviting and distributing contributions, probing and redirecting, signalling stages and time, and closing with a fair summary. Facilitation is commonly assessed in student-led seminars and is a mediation skill that requires attending to others' participation and the development of ideas as much as to one's own content.
masteryEvidence: Opens by framing the task and posing an open question that participants can answer from their preparation
Invites contributions from quieter participants without putting them on the spot (e.g. advance notice, rounds, pair-then-share)
Uses follow-up probes to deepen contributions and redirects digressions back to the task
Signals stages and manages time so that all planned questions are addressed
Closes with a summary of positions and outcomes that participants accept as accurate
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to facilitate a 12-minute discussion of a set reading with four peers while an observer maps who speaks to whom. Check the opening question, spread of participation, follow-up probes, time management and the closing summary; partial facilitation asks prepared questions in sequence without following up; a gap is the facilitator dominating the content or the discussion stalling.

topics.name: Summarising discussion
topics.description: Summarise a discussion orally or in brief notes by selecting the main positions, points of agreement and disagreement, unresolved questions and outcomes, organising them thematically and attributing them fairly. Summarising consolidates co-constructed understanding and is required when groups report back to a class or when a facilitator closes a discussion.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the main positions expressed rather than listing every contribution
States points of agreement and disagreement and attributes them accurately
Names at least one unresolved question or next step
Delivers a 60–90-second report-back that participants recognise as fair
Organises the summary thematically with spoken signposts rather than chronologically
topics.assessmentPrompt: After a 10-minute discussion, give the learner two minutes to prepare a 60-second report-back for another group. Check selectivity, fair representation of differing views, mention of an unresolved issue and clear organisation; a gap response is a chronological list of who said what, or the learner's own view presented as the group's conclusion.

topics.name: Managing speaking anxiety and willingness to communicate
topics.description: Understand speaking anxiety and willingness to communicate (WTC) as situational and changeable — shaped by preparation, task familiarity, group relations, how the floor is distributed and perceived evaluation — and use preparation and in-the-moment strategies to participate. Treating reticence as a product of conditions rather than a fixed personal or cultural trait lets learners and teachers change the conditions as well as the behaviour.
masteryEvidence: Identifies specific situations and factors that raise or lower their own willingness to speak
Uses at least two strategies to participate despite anxiety (e.g. a prepared opening move, an early low-stakes contribution, note prompts, deliberate pausing)
Sets and reviews a concrete participation goal across a series of sessions
Distinguishes choosing silence for a reason from being unable to enter the discussion
Negotiates alternative or graded routes to participation (e.g. a written post first, a defined role in small groups) when needed
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to place three recent discussion situations on a 'willing to speak' scale and explain what made each easier or harder. Strong responses identify situational factors (preparation, group, tutor moves, topic) and name strategies used or planned; a gap response attributes reticence wholly to a fixed trait ('I'm a shy person', 'people from my background don't speak') with no actionable strategy.

topics.name: Synchronous online discussion
topics.description: Participate in synchronous online and hybrid seminars by using raise-hand, chat and reaction functions to bid for and supplement turns, compensating for reduced gaze and gesture and for audio delay with explicit addressing, yielding and confirmation, and organising breakout-room tasks. Online discussion changes how turns are taken and how participation is made visible, so face-to-face strategies need adapting.
masteryEvidence: Bids for turns using the platform's conventions and enters promptly when invited
Addresses contributions to named participants and yields turns explicitly to compensate for missing gaze and gesture cues
Uses the chat to add sources, questions or brief responses without derailing the spoken discussion
Organises breakout tasks by agreeing a reporter and timekeeper and recording outcomes
Recovers from technical disruption by summarising what was missed and checking before continuing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Review a recorded 15-minute online seminar with the learner, looking at both spoken turns and chat contributions. Check for appropriate bidding, explicit addressing and yielding, purposeful chat use and recovery from disruption; a gap is a learner who contributes only in the chat or not at all, or who repeatedly talks over others because of delay.

topics.name: Structured academic debate
topics.description: Take part in structured academic debates by building a case within a time limit, anticipating and rebutting the strongest opposing arguments, conceding where necessary and responding concisely to challenges. Debate trains rapid oral argument, but its adversarial logic differs from the exploratory, idea-developing norms of most seminars, and learners need to know when each mode is appropriate.
masteryEvidence: Delivers a timed constructive speech with a clear claim, two or three supported arguments and a summary
Rebuts a specific opposing argument by identifying a weak premise, missing warrant or inadequate evidence
Concedes a valid opposing point while showing why the overall case still holds
Responds to a challenge or point of information concisely without losing the thread of the speech
Explains how debate norms differ from those of exploratory seminar discussion
topics.assessmentPrompt: After the opposing side's speech, give the learner two minutes to prepare a 90-second rebuttal. Check whether they target the strongest opposing argument rather than a peripheral one, explain why it fails, concede where appropriate and summarise their case; a gap response restates their own case without engaging the opposition.

dependencies.reason: Reading what a group task assesses depends on understanding assessment types, learning outcomes and how marks are allocated
Roles and milestones are planned against what the task assesses and whether it requires cooperation or collaboration
Breaking a group task into parts begins with unpacking the brief, scope and criteria
Setting realistic internal milestones applies individual planning and prioritising skills to a shared timeline
Meetings track progress against an agreed plan, roles and milestones
Chairing an agenda item draws on facilitation moves such as inviting views, redirecting and summarising
Minutes and action points are a form of shared, co-constructed notes
Raising concerns and negotiating solutions requires mitigated but clear disagreement
Agreed ground rules and roles provide the shared reference point for raising process concerns
Distinguishing genuine conflict from differences in communicative expectations draws on intercultural awareness
Accommodating to varied accents and proficiency rests on understanding communicative effectiveness among multilingual users of English
Widening participation requires understanding how turns are gained and lost in group talk
Co-authoring depends on an agreed structure, division of sections and internal deadlines
Shared documents, comments and track changes are the usual tools of student co-authoring
Integrating separately drafted sections is a whole-text revision of argument and structure
Co-authoring requires knowing where legitimate collaboration ends and individually assessed work begins
Evaluating contributions applies criterion-referenced self- and peer-assessment to group work
Minutes and action-point records provide the evidence on which fair contribution judgements are based
Individual accounts of one's role are often written as structured reflective commentaries
Adapting a talk to its audience applies the idea that field, tenor and mode shape language choices
Learners usually meet audience and purpose analysis first in writing, and the presentation version extends it to live listeners
Selecting and ordering main points depends on the purpose and what the audience needs
Designing for real-time listening requires understanding how spoken and written packaging of information differ
Outlining a structure from a position and evidence is usually taught first for writing and then adapted for speech
An opening previews and frames a structure that must already be planned
Audience engagement in openings uses resources such as inclusive pronouns, questions and appeals to shared knowledge
Signposts announce and mark transitions between parts of a structure the speaker has planned
Presentation signposting applies the general repertoire of spoken macro- and micro-markers to monologue
Slides should follow the talk's structure, one main point per slide, so structure is planned first
Choosing and simplifying charts for slides applies principles of chart choice and honest design
Accessible slides apply general principles of contrast, readable type and alternatives to colour-coded meaning
Talking through data adapts the location–highlight–interpretation moves of data commentary to speech
Explaining data aloud requires saying numbers, decimals, ranges and units intelligibly
Visuals that have been simplified and built for presentation are far easier to talk through
Highlighting key and contrastive information in a talk depends on control of nuclear stress
Signalling continuation, completion and engagement draws on tone choice
Appropriate non-verbal behaviour depends on the setting, audience size and formality
Interpreting and adapting gaze and gesture norms draws on awareness that communicative expectations vary
The case for prompts rather than scripts rests on the lexical density of written language being hard to process aurally
Prompts encode a planned structure, which must exist before notes can be reduced to cues
Formulating sentences in real time from prompts relies on fluency resources such as formulaic sequences and planning routines
Answering well begins with confirming or reformulating the question, a confirmation-check skill
Acknowledging limits and answering critical questions requires spoken hedging and stance resources
Q&A is the least predictable, most anxiety-provoking phase, so strategies for managing anxiety support composure and retrieval
A coherent group talk depends on agreeing roles, a shared plan and internal deadlines
Handovers between speakers are signposting moves that summarise and preview across sections
Integration and timing across several speakers are achieved mainly through joint rehearsal
Presenting a poster presupposes a poster whose layout and reading path the presenter understands and can use
Poster sessions consist largely of visitor questions and comments, so Q&A skills are central
Guiding visitors through figures on the poster uses the orient–highlight–interpret routine
Conference introductions combine context, argument and audience-engagement moves taught in openings
In research presentations much of the argument is carried by visuals the presenter must talk through
Discussion sessions after research talks are a defining part of the genre
Strict conference time limits make rehearsed timing and pre-planned cuts essential
Framing a talk's contribution draws on the written moves for indicating a gap and occupying a niche
Without live visual contact, a recorded talk depends heavily on clear, engaging vocal delivery
Screen-shared slides dominate the viewer's field of view, so slide design matters even more
Recorded formats tempt speakers to read a script on screen, so speaking from prompts is a key safeguard
Timing checkpoints and planned cuts are set section by section against a planned structure
Rehearsal cycles are one application of practice routines for reducing hesitation
The rehearse–evaluate–adjust cycle is an instance of forethought, performance and self-reflection
Seminar participation norms are a concrete instance of broader expectations of independent, critical and active engagement
What counts as adequate preparation depends on knowing what the seminar is for and how contributions are judged
Seminar preparation notes extend reading notes that keep source details and separate the author's claims from the reader's comments
Preparing questions and positions draws on routines for interrogating a text's claims, evidence and implications
Learners cannot find transition points or judge when to enter until they can track speakers, positions and turns in multi-party talk
Judging when interruption or overlap is acceptable draws on understanding of face and imposition
Justifying a view orally requires the language of giving reasons and rationales
Understanding argument as a reasoned position supported by evidence underpins the claim–reason–support contribution
Disagreeing productively requires being able to state and justify an alternative position
Mitigated and partial disagreement depends on spoken stance and hedging resources
Calibrating mitigation to relationship and stakes applies concepts of face and power distance
Extending or qualifying a peer's point requires the learner to contribute a supported idea of their own
Accurately reformulating a peer's point is the first step of building on it
Linking moves must be made at the right moment, while the relevant point is still the focus of discussion
Targeted clarification questions depend on monitoring comprehension and locating what was not understood
Choosing direct or mitigated question forms to tutors and peers applies understanding of face and imposition
Substantive questions about evidence and implications draw on habits of critical questioning
Confirmation checks are a specialised form of clarification question
Reformulating one's own unclear point uses self-repair and paraphrase strategies
Sources are cited in discussion to support or challenge a position, so the learner must be able to state one
Oral attribution adapts written signal phrases and the marking of where attributed content ends
Citing readings in real time depends on having noted claims and locators during preparation
Summarising a discussion requires tracking how contributions relate to one another and synthesising them
Report-backs use the language of summarising and drawing conclusions
Summarising depends on noting main positions selectively during the discussion rather than transcribing
Facilitators must summarise at transitions and at the close, and must track how contributions relate
Distributing turns equitably applies an understanding of how participation is shaped in multilingual groups
Clarifying what is expected in seminars reduces uncertainty, one source of anxiety, and frames realistic participation goals
Analysing one's own willingness to communicate draws on knowledge of oneself as a learner and of available strategies
Online turn-taking adapts face-to-face floor-taking and yielding to platform conventions and reduced cues
Reduced visual feedback and audio problems make explicit confirmation checks more necessary online
Appropriate use of cameras, microphones and chat builds on general norms of online academic conduct
Debate is a formalised, time-limited application of constructing and defending arguments in speech
Rebuttal and concession are the defining moves of the debate format
Learners need to understand advocacy as distinct from exploratory inquiry to use debate appropriately and not transfer its norms to seminars

guidance.summary: Ferris and Tagg (1996) found that oral and interactive course requirements vary considerably by discipline, and Leki (2001) found group projects in courses across the curriculum but little instructor guidance on how students should collaborate. Teach learners to read assessment briefs for what is marked (product, process, individual contribution), to distinguish cooperation (division of labour) from collaboration (joint construction), and to locate rules on permitted collaboration.

activities.title: Decoding the group brief
learnerActions: Read a real group assignment brief and highlight what is assessed and how marks are split
Identify any individual components (e.g. reflections, peer evaluation) and their weighting
List questions to ask the module leader where the brief is unclear
activities.intendedInsight: Group tasks differ in what they assess, and reading the brief closely shapes how a group should work.
activities.rationale: Makes explicit the variation in course requirements that Ferris and Tagg (1996) report and that students otherwise discover late.

activities.title: Cooperation or collaboration?
learnerActions: Classify six short task descriptions as needing division of labour, joint construction or both
Discuss what would go wrong if a joint-construction task were simply divided
Apply the distinction to a current or upcoming group task
activities.intendedInsight: Some tasks cannot be done well by dividing them up.
activities.rationale: Counters the 'divide and staple' approach that leaves group outputs fragmented.

difficulties.pattern: 'Group work is unfair because my mark depends on other people.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to engage; attempts to do all the work alone or to minimise involvement.
difficulties.response: Show how individual components and peer evaluation affect marks, and discuss the purposes of group work. Acknowledge that the concern can be legitimate where assessment design is weak.

difficulties.pattern: Treating every group task as a division of labour.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sections written independently and combined just before the deadline.
difficulties.response: Use the cooperation–collaboration distinction and plan joint stages (shared planning, integration edit, joint rehearsal).

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, from a brief, what will be assessed and how their individual mark will be decided.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurately describes product, process and individual components and their weighting.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the product but not individual components.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes everyone gets the same mark for the final product.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners may meet assessed group work for the first time. Pre-sessional learners should be prepared for the group assessments in their target disciplines. In-sessional UG and PGT learners apply this to current module briefs.
reviewNotes: Leki (2001) and Ferris and Tagg (1996) are US-based; group assessment practices differ across institutions and countries.

guidance.summary: Leki's (2001) account of multilingual students being given marginal roles in group projects suggests that role allocation should be explicit and negotiated rather than left to assumptions about who is competent. The Companion Volume's goal-oriented co-operation scale describes the language of planning joint action (Council of Europe, 2020). Teach task breakdown from the brief, ground rules, role allocation by expertise and development, and milestone planning.

activities.title: Ground-rules charter
learnerActions: In the first meeting, agree rules on communication channels, response times, decision-making and what happens when deadlines are missed
Write the rules in a shared document and have every member confirm them
Review and revise the charter at the project's midpoint
activities.intendedInsight: Explicit rules give the group a neutral reference point when problems arise.
activities.rationale: Addresses the lack of collaboration guidance Leki (2001) observed by making group norms explicit.

activities.title: Backwards milestone plan
learnerActions: Start from the submission date and work backwards to set internal deadlines for drafts, integration and rehearsal
Assign an owner to each milestone
Identify the riskiest dependency and plan a buffer for it
activities.intendedInsight: Internal deadlines and integration time must be planned, not left to the end.
activities.rationale: Practises the planning language and joint decision-making described in goal-oriented co-operation scales (Council of Europe, 2020).

difficulties.pattern: Roles allocated by assumed language ability (e.g. multilingual members given formatting or slide design only).
difficulties.revealedBy: Some members have no substantive content role; they report feeling sidelined.
difficulties.response: Discuss Leki's (2001) findings with the whole group, allocate by expertise and development goals, and rotate roles where possible.

difficulties.pattern: No internal deadlines; all work converges on the final week.
difficulties.revealedBy: Last-minute integration and missing sections.
difficulties.response: Require dated milestones in the plan and check them at review points.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting a peripheral role to avoid conflict or exposure.
difficulties.revealedBy: A member volunteers only for low-visibility tasks and contributes little to content.
difficulties.response: Encourage members to state development goals in the planning meeting and give them language for negotiating roles.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show their group's plan and explain how roles were decided.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A written plan with ground rules, negotiated roles and internal milestones.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Roles assigned but no ground rules or internal deadlines.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No plan; the work is divided by word count.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from templates for plans and charters. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners apply them to real projects; PGT learners often have little time to form groups, so a fast planning routine is valuable.

guidance.summary: Effective group meetings make decisions and responsibilities visible. The Companion Volume describes formal discussion in meetings and managing interaction as part of interaction and mediation competence (Council of Europe, 2020). There is little EAP research specifically on student project meetings, so teaching draws on practitioner models: agenda, chairing, decision language and action-point minutes.

activities.title: From agenda to action points
learnerActions: Draft a three-item agenda with a purpose and time for each item
Hold a 15-minute meeting with a rotating chair and timekeeper
Write minutes listing only decisions and action points with owners and deadlines
activities.intendedInsight: A meeting is productive when it ends with recorded decisions and actions.
activities.rationale: Practises the meeting functions captured in formal discussion and managing-interaction scales (Council of Europe, 2020).

activities.title: Minutes comparison
learnerActions: Compare narrative minutes ('X said… then Y said…') with action-point minutes of the same meeting
Identify which version would help a member who missed the meeting
Rewrite narrative minutes as action points
activities.intendedInsight: Minutes record outcomes, not conversation.
activities.rationale: Contrasting models makes the function of minutes explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Meetings drift without decisions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated discussion of the same issues across meetings.
difficulties.response: Assign a chair, use an agenda and practise proposing and confirming decisions.

difficulties.pattern: Minutes narrate the discussion and omit decisions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long minutes with no clear actions or owners.
difficulties.response: Provide an action-point template and practise summarising decisions.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner for the minutes of their last group meeting.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Decisions and action points with owners and deadlines.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some decisions recorded, but no owners or dates.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No minutes, or a narrative of the discussion.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and in-sessional UG learners apply meeting routines to assessed projects. PGT learners often meet online across time zones. PGR researchers attend research-team and supervisory meetings, where agendas and action points support progress.
reviewNotes: No listed EAP study focuses on student project meetings; guidance is practitioner-based.

guidance.summary: Group-work conflict often concerns process (deadlines, workload, communication) rather than ideas, and Leki (2001) documents tensions and unequal treatment in multilingual project groups. Politeness theory (Brown & Levinson, 1987) helps explain how face-threatening concerns can be raised with mitigation while remaining clear. Teach early, specific, ground-rule-referenced raising of concerns, negotiation and proportionate escalation.

activities.title: Observation, impact, request
learnerActions: Write a concern using three parts: a specific observation, its impact on the group, and a request or proposal
Role-play raising it in a meeting, with the other person responding
Discuss how mitigation affected clarity and the response
activities.intendedInsight: A concern can be raised clearly without being accusatory.
activities.rationale: Applies face-saving mitigation (Brown & Levinson, 1987) to a high-stakes, face-threatening act.

activities.title: Escalation ladder
learnerActions: List steps from informal conversation to involving the module leader
Decide what evidence is needed at each step
Draft a short, factual message to a tutor for the final step
activities.intendedInsight: Escalation is proportionate, evidenced and staged.
activities.rationale: Gives learners a procedure for the situations of unequal contribution and treatment that Leki (2001) documents.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding raising problems until the deadline.
difficulties.revealedBy: Late complaints to tutors; the work is incomplete.
difficulties.response: Build in checkpoints where concerns are routinely raised, and practise early, low-key raising.

difficulties.pattern: Accusatory or emotional messages to group members or tutors.
difficulties.revealedBy: Escalating conflict; tutor intervention needed.
difficulties.response: Practise the observation–impact–request structure and mitigated language.

difficulties.pattern: Interpreting different communication styles (e.g. directness, response times) as rudeness or disengagement.
difficulties.revealedBy: Complaints about tone rather than substance.
difficulties.response: Discuss variation in communicative expectations and agree group norms explicitly.

diagnostic.task: Present a scenario in which a member is not contributing and ask how the learner would handle it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Early, specific, ground-rule-referenced raising, a proposed solution and staged escalation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Appropriate concern but vague or late.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Avoidance or immediate complaint to the tutor without evidence.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners practise in short projects. In-sessional UG and PGT learners face real conflicts with marks at stake. PGR researchers manage disagreements in research teams and co-authorship, where power differences are greater.

guidance.summary: Leki (2001) found multilingual undergraduates in group projects positioned as less capable and allocated peripheral roles, and Morita (2004) shows how positioning shapes participation in graduate classrooms. Research on English as a lingua franca in international universities reframes communicative success as mutual accommodation rather than conformity to native-speaker norms (Jenkins, 2014). Inclusive collaboration is therefore a competence for all students, including home students and the most proficient English users, and is also supported by task design.

activities.title: Accommodation audit
learnerActions: Record a short group discussion
Each member identifies one moment where their own speech (speed, idiom, local reference) may have made understanding harder
Agree two accommodation practices for the group
activities.intendedInsight: Intelligibility is a shared responsibility of speakers and listeners.
activities.rationale: Applies ELF research on mutual accommodation (Jenkins, 2014) to group practice.

activities.title: Trying participation structures
learnerActions: Hold one discussion as open talk and one using rounds with written input first
Map who spoke and whose ideas were taken up in each
Decide which structures to use for which group tasks
activities.intendedInsight: Participation structures change who contributes.
activities.rationale: Addresses the positioning effects documented by Leki (2001) and Morita (2004) through design rather than exhortation.

difficulties.pattern: 'They can't contribute much because their English isn't good enough.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Peers allocate peripheral tasks or ignore suggestions from some members.
difficulties.response: Discuss evidence of positioning (Leki, 2001), separate language proficiency from expertise, and allocate content roles to all.

difficulties.pattern: Proficient or confident speakers dominating without realising it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Participation maps show one or two members taking most turns.
difficulties.response: Share participation data with the group and practise inviting and building on others.

difficulties.pattern: Multilingual members withdrawing to avoid exposure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Members volunteer only for invisible tasks.
difficulties.response: Create low-risk entry points (written input, pairs) and invite specific expertise.

diagnostic.task: Show a transcript of a group meeting in which one member is overlooked and ask what the learner notices and would do.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the exclusion and proposes concrete, tactful moves and structures.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices the problem but frames it as the overlooked member's language deficit.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Notices nothing problematic.

guidance.contextNotes: Relevant at every stage. Foundation and pre-sessional groups are often all multilingual, so practise accommodation among varied Englishes. In-sessional UG and PGT groups mix home and international students, where awareness among more proficient users is critical. PGR teams are often international.

guidance.summary: Collaborative writing requires coordinating text, not only dividing tasks; Leki (2001) shows group projects often resulting in fragmented division of labour. Classroom research on collaborative writing among L2 learners suggests that writing jointly can prompt discussion of both ideas and language (Storch, 2005). Teach agreed structures and style sheets, shared-document workflows, integrating edits and the boundary with individually assessed work.

activities.title: Group style sheet
learnerActions: Agree key terms and their definitions, tense conventions and the citation style
Record them in a one-page style sheet at the top of the shared document
Check each section against the style sheet before integration
activities.intendedInsight: Consistency across authors must be agreed, not assumed.
activities.rationale: Coordinates the text-level choices that separately drafted sections otherwise leave inconsistent.

activities.title: Integration edit
learnerActions: Each member reads the whole draft and comments on links between sections
The group meets to agree transitions and cut repetition
One member makes a final consistency pass while others check references
activities.intendedInsight: Integration is a joint revision stage that needs time in the plan.
activities.rationale: Draws on evidence that joint writing prompts collaborative attention to ideas and language (Storch, 2005).

difficulties.pattern: Sections pasted together at the last minute.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent style, repetition and no transitions.
difficulties.response: Schedule an integration milestone well before submission.

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to edit peers' text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comments only, or no edits; inconsistent final text.
difficulties.response: Agree editing norms and use suggestion mode so that changes are visible and negotiable.
