difficulties.pattern: Uncertainty about whether help with individually assessed parts is allowed.
difficulties.revealedBy: Shared drafts of individual reflections; questions about collusion.
difficulties.response: Clarify the brief's rules on individual components with the module team.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe how their group will turn separate sections into a single report.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes a style sheet, an integration stage, shared tools and a final consistency check.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions a final proofread only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes sections will simply be combined.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and in-sessional UG learners co-write reports and proposals. PGT learners co-write consultancy-style or business reports. PGR researchers co-author papers, where contributor roles and authorship conventions also matter.
reviewNotes: Storch (2005) is a proposed reference not yet in the bibliography; it concerns pair writing in class rather than extended group projects, so its relevance is indirect.

guidance.summary: Evaluative judgement depends on understanding criteria and comparing work against them (Sadler, 1989). Peer evaluation of contributions can reproduce the positioning Leki (2001) documented, in which multilingual members' contributions were undervalued. Teach criterion-referenced, evidenced evaluation and accurate self-documentation.

activities.title: Evidence-based rating
learnerActions: Read anonymised minutes and a version history for a group project
Rate each member against the given criteria, citing evidence for each rating
Compare ratings with peers and discuss where and why they differ
activities.intendedInsight: Fair judgements rest on criteria and evidence rather than impressions.
activities.rationale: Applies Sadler's (1989) account of evaluative judgement against criteria to peer evaluation.

activities.title: Contribution statement
learnerActions: Write a 150-word statement of your own contribution, citing evidence
Include one limitation and what you would do differently
Exchange statements with a group member and check them against shared records
activities.intendedInsight: Accurate self-reporting includes evidence and limitations.
activities.rationale: Builds the self-documentation skills individual reflective components require.

difficulties.pattern: Rating contribution by how much someone talked in meetings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Low ratings for members who did substantial written or research work.
difficulties.response: Separate visibility from contribution and use evidence from task logs and version history.

difficulties.pattern: Under-reporting one's own contribution.
difficulties.revealedBy: Vague or modest self-statements that omit significant work.
difficulties.response: Model evidenced statements and give language for describing contributions accurately.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to rate two group members on given criteria and justify the ratings.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Criterion-based ratings with specific evidence, including less visible work.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Ratings with general justifications.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equal ratings with no justification, or ratings based on friendship or talk.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional programmes introduce peer evaluation in short projects. In-sessional UG and PGT modules often use peer moderation of group marks, so fairness and evidence matter for grades.

guidance.summary: Research on academic presentations shows speakers shaping their talk to the audience: conference introductions combine contextual, argumentative and interactional moves (Rowley-Jolivet & Carter-Thomas, 2005), and presenters use interpersonal resources to engage listeners (Hood & Forey, 2005). Morita (2000) shows that what counts as a successful presentation is learned through socialisation into a particular community. Teach audience analysis as a planning step that changes content and selection, not only register.

activities.title: Same study, two audiences
learnerActions: Read a short study summary from your field
Plan a 3-minute talk on it for specialists and another for students from a different discipline
Compare the two plans: what was added, omitted, defined or exemplified differently, and why
activities.intendedInsight: Audience changes what you say, not only how formally you say it.
activities.rationale: Makes concrete the audience-oriented choices that Rowley-Jolivet and Carter-Thomas (2005) identify in conference introductions.

activities.title: Audience questions first
learnerActions: Before planning, list five questions the audience is likely to have about the topic
Check that the plan answers the most important ones and drop content that answers none
After presenting, compare the predicted questions with those actually asked
activities.intendedInsight: Content selection can be driven by audience needs rather than by everything the speaker knows.
activities.rationale: Builds understanding of audience expectations as part of learning a community's presentation norms, as Morita (2000) describes.

difficulties.pattern: 'I need to show the teacher everything I know.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Overloaded content, rapid delivery and overruns; slides crowded with detail.
difficulties.response: Make the audience and purpose explicit in the task brief and assess selection as a criterion. Show that a focused talk demonstrates understanding more convincingly than coverage.

difficulties.pattern: Treating audience adaptation as changing greetings, contractions and formality only.
difficulties.revealedBy: Specialist and non-specialist versions of a talk differ only in surface formality.
difficulties.response: Compare paired versions of a talk in which terminology, background and examples change, and ask learners to identify each change.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Who is your audience, what do they already know, and what should they remember after your talk?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes the audience's knowledge specifically, states a focused purpose and links both to content decisions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the audience generally ('my classmates') and a broad topic rather than a purpose.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot say who the audience is or what they should take away.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners work with peer audiences and simple purposes. Pre-sessional learners address mixed-discipline audiences of peers and assessors. In-sessional UG and PGT learners adapt to module audiences; PGR researchers must adapt the same research to specialist, interdisciplinary and public audiences.

guidance.summary: Listeners process a presentation once, in real time, so explicit macro-structure matters: Chaudron and Richards (1986) found that macro-markers signalling lecture organisation aided listeners' recall, and Thompson (2003) shows lecturers signalling structure through both words and intonation. Speech and writing package information differently (Halliday, 1989), so presentations built paragraph by paragraph from an essay are hard to follow. Teach fewer main points, roadmaps and internal summaries.

activities.title: Essay to talk
learnerActions: Take a short essay you have written
Reduce it to three main points, each with one key support
Add a roadmap, internal summaries and a conclusion that returns to the purpose, then deliver it in four minutes
activities.intendedInsight: A presentation is restructured for listeners, not a spoken version of an essay.
activities.rationale: Applies the difference between written and spoken packaging of information (Halliday, 1989) to a familiar text.

activities.title: The listener's map
learnerActions: Listen to a peer's talk without slides and sketch its structure
Compare your sketch with the speaker's plan
Discuss where and why the structure was lost
activities.intendedInsight: Structure exists for listeners only if it is audible.
activities.rationale: Gives speakers direct evidence of the comprehension benefit of explicit macro-structure reported by Chaudron and Richards (1986).

difficulties.pattern: Including too many main points for the time available.
difficulties.revealedBy: Eight or more 'main points', rushed endings and no internal summaries.
difficulties.response: Set a maximum number of main points and practise grouping related ideas under one point.

difficulties.pattern: Following the written essay's structure and wording verbatim.
difficulties.revealedBy: The outline mirrors essay paragraphs; there is no roadmap or summary because the essay had none.
difficulties.response: Contrast reader and listener needs explicitly and require a spoken redesign of the structure.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show the plan for their next presentation and explain how the audience will know where they are at each stage.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A focused plan with a roadmap, internal summaries and time allocations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A clear sequence of points but no roadmap or summaries.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A list of slides with no overall structure.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit from a clear default structure. In-sessional UG and PGT learners adapt structure to disciplinary formats (e.g. case presentations, design reviews, project pitches).
reviewNotes: Chaudron and Richards (1986) and Thompson (2003) study lectures, not student presentations; the transfer to presentations rests on the shared demands of extended academic monologue.

guidance.summary: Rowley-Jolivet and Carter-Thomas (2005) show that conference presentation introductions combine setting up context, establishing the argument and interacting with the audience. Hood and Forey (2005) show presenters using interpersonal resources, including evaluation and humour, to build solidarity with the audience. Teach openings as a repertoire of moves to select and order for the audience and genre, rather than a fixed formula of greeting, name and topic.

activities.title: Opening move analysis
learnerActions: Watch the first two minutes of three academic talks in your field (e.g. recorded conference or departmental talks)
Label the moves used: context, relevance, purpose or claim, preview, audience engagement
Compare the order and length of moves across the three talks
activities.intendedInsight: Openings are built from identifiable moves that expert speakers combine flexibly.
activities.rationale: Applies the context–argument–interaction framework from Rowley-Jolivet and Carter-Thomas (2005) to authentic models.

activities.title: Three alternative openings
learnerActions: Write three openings for the same talk, starting respectively with a question, a problem and a striking finding
Deliver each to a small group
The group chooses the most engaging opening and explains why
activities.intendedInsight: Interpersonal engagement can be designed and tested.
activities.rationale: Practises the interpersonal resources Hood and Forey (2005) identify in presentation introductions.

difficulties.pattern: Opening with a long self-introduction or an apology ('Sorry for my English').
difficulties.revealedBy: The first 30–60 seconds contain no purpose; apologies lower the audience's expectations.
difficulties.response: Discuss the effect of apologies on credibility and practise starting with relevance. Acknowledge nerves rather than forbidding any reference to them.

difficulties.pattern: Adding a rhetorical question or 'hook' unrelated to the talk's purpose.
difficulties.revealedBy: An attention-grabbing question that the talk never returns to.
difficulties.response: Require every engagement move to link to the purpose and be revisited in the conclusion.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to deliver the first 60 seconds of a talk, then ask a listener to state its purpose and predict its structure.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The listener can state the purpose and predict the structure; an engagement move links to the purpose.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Purpose is clear but there is no preview or engagement.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The listener cannot say what the talk is for.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need a reliable default opening. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners adapt openings to the task and audience. PGR researchers work with conference introductions that position the study within a field and establish rapport with specialist audiences.

guidance.summary: Thompson (2003) shows lecturers signalling organisation through both lexical metadiscourse and intonation, Chaudron and Richards (1986) found that macro-markers aided listeners' recall of lectures, and Deroey and Taverniers (2012) describe the lexicogrammatical markers lecturers use to flag important points. Teach lexical and prosodic signalling together, and treat density as a choice rather than maximising the number of markers.

activities.title: Signpost and pause
learnerActions: Mark the section boundaries in your plan and write a transition for each
Mark a pause and a pitch reset at each boundary
Record the talk and check whether a listener can hear the boundaries
activities.intendedInsight: Signposting is prosodic as well as lexical.
activities.rationale: Reflects Thompson's (2003) evidence that intonation and pausing contribute to signalling organisation.

activities.title: Marking what matters
learnerActions: Identify the single most important point in each section
Mark it with a relevance marker and prosodic emphasis
Ask listeners afterwards to recall the key point of each section
activities.intendedInsight: Listeners remember what speakers explicitly flag as important.
activities.rationale: Draws on Deroey and Taverniers's (2012) description of relevance markers in lectures.

difficulties.pattern: Using the same memorised formula at every transition ('Now I would like to move on to my next point').
difficulties.revealedBy: Repetitive markers that sound mechanical; signposts outnumber content statements.
difficulties.response: Teach a range of transitions, including content-based ones that summarise and preview, and reduce density for short talks.

difficulties.pattern: Delivering signposts without pausing or changing pitch, so boundaries are inaudible.
difficulties.revealedBy: Listeners cannot reconstruct the structure despite correct lexical markers.
difficulties.response: Practise pausing before and after major transitions and recording to check audibility.

diagnostic.task: Ask a listener to sketch the structure of a 3-minute recorded section of the learner's talk.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The sketch matches the plan; transitions are marked lexically and prosodically.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Markers present but boundaries blurred by continuous delivery.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No discernible structure.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need a core repertoire. In-sessional learners refine density and variety and adapt signposting to group handovers and recorded formats.
reviewNotes: The cited studies concern lectures; the guidance assumes similar listener needs in student presentations.

guidance.summary: In scientific conference presentations, visuals are central to how the argument is made rather than decorative (Rowley-Jolivet, 2002). Principles of visual composition such as salience, framing and information value help explain how audiences read slides (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006), and Tufte's (2001) principle of minimising non-data elements in graphics applies to charts on slides. Accessible design follows recognised standards for contrast and for not relying on colour alone (W3C, 2023). Teach slides as support for speech: the speaker carries the explanation; slides carry the point, key terms and evidence.

activities.title: Slide makeover
learnerActions: Take one of your own text-heavy slides
Rewrite the heading as a statement of the slide's point and move explanatory sentences to speaker notes
Simplify any chart by removing non-essential elements and highlighting the feature you will discuss
activities.intendedInsight: A slide supports speech best when it shows the point and the evidence, not the script.
activities.rationale: Applies principles of salience (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006) and of reducing non-data elements (Tufte, 2001).

activities.title: Accessibility check
learnerActions: Check text–background contrast with a contrast-checking tool and test font sizes from the back of the room
Identify any meaning carried by colour alone and add labels or patterns
Add alternative text to figures in slides that will be shared
activities.intendedInsight: Accessible slides are clearer for everyone.
activities.rationale: Applies widely used accessibility criteria (W3C, 2023) to presentation slides.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I put everything on the slide, I won't forget anything and the audience can read it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Full sentences and paragraphs on slides; the speaker reads them aloud.
difficulties.response: Move text to speaker notes and practise speaking from prompts, keeping slides for the point and evidence. Do not strip all text at once from anxious presenters.

difficulties.pattern: Decorative templates, animations and stock images that are unrelated to the content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Visual elements that compete with or do not relate to the message.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to justify every visual element by its function; remove those that have none.

difficulties.pattern: Pasting complex figures from published papers without simplification.
difficulties.revealedBy: Illegible axes, multiple panels and no indication of what the audience should look at.
difficulties.response: Teach simplifying, cropping or rebuilding figures and highlighting the relevant feature, with attribution.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to talk you through three of their slides, saying what each slide's point is and what the audience should look at.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Each slide has a clear point stated in the heading, minimal text and a focused visual.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Points are clear in speech but not on the slides, or visuals are not simplified.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Slides are pages of text that the learner reads aloud.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on basic text economy and legibility. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners add data visuals and accessibility. PGR researchers design for conference conditions and disciplinary conventions, for example dense results slides in some sciences.
reviewNotes: Popular slide 'rules' (e.g. fixed numbers of bullets or words per slide) lack a strong research base and are deliberately not presented as rules here.
W3C (2023) concerns web content; its contrast and use-of-colour criteria are applied to slides by analogy.

guidance.summary: Rowley-Jolivet (2002) shows that visuals carry much of the argument in scientific conference presentations, and the CEFR Companion Volume treats explaining data in graphs and diagrams as a mediation activity (Council of Europe, 2020). The written data-commentary moves of locating, highlighting and interpreting (Swales & Feak, 2012) transfer to speech, with an added need to orient listeners first and to synchronise speech with pointing.

activities.title: Orient, highlight, interpret
learnerActions: For a chart from your field, write one orienting sentence (what it shows, axes, units)
Choose the one or two features that matter and say what they mean for your argument
Deliver the explanation in 60 seconds and ask listeners what they would remember
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining a visual means selecting and interpreting, not describing everything.
activities.rationale: Adapts the data-commentary moves described by Swales and Feak (2012) for listeners.

activities.title: Point and speak
learnerActions: Rehearse explaining a complex figure while pointing to each element as you mention it
Use slide builds to reveal the figure in stages
Compare audience comprehension with and without builds
activities.intendedInsight: Synchronising speech and visual attention reduces audience effort.
activities.rationale: Responds to the central argumentative role of visuals in research presentations (Rowley-Jolivet, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: Reading out every value in the chart.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long lists of numbers with no interpretation.
difficulties.response: Limit learners to two highlighted features and require a 'so what' statement.

difficulties.pattern: Errors saying numbers aloud (e.g. thirteen/thirty, decimals, large numbers).
difficulties.revealedBy: Listener confusion about quantities; mismatch between spoken and displayed figures.
difficulties.response: Practise saying the specific numbers in the talk and round where precision is unnecessary.

difficulties.pattern: Talking about a visual before it appears, or after moving on to the next slide.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mismatch between what is said and what is shown.
difficulties.response: Rehearse with the slides and plan builds; pause to let the audience look before explaining.

diagnostic.task: Show an unfamiliar chart for one minute and ask for a 60-second explanation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Orients, highlights one to three features and interprets them, with accurate numbers.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate description but no interpretation, or interpretation without orientation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Reads values left to right or misreads the chart.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners practise with simple charts. In-sessional UG and PGT learners explain disciplinary visuals; PGR researchers explain their own complex results, often under time pressure.

guidance.summary: Intelligibility-oriented pronunciation teaching prioritises features that most affect listeners' understanding rather than native-like accent (Derwing & Munro, 2015). Hahn (2004) found that appropriate primary stress in a recorded lecture improved listeners' recall and their evaluations of the speaker, and Pickering (2001) found that international teaching assistants' tone choices shaped how engaging and comprehensible their teaching was perceived to be. Focus delivery work on thought groups, prominence, pace and intonation.

activities.title: Mark up and deliver
learnerActions: Mark thought-group boundaries and prominent words on a one-minute section of your talk
Record it and listen for whether prominence falls on new and contrastive information
Re-record after revising the marking
activities.intendedInsight: Where stress and pauses fall changes how easily listeners follow.
activities.rationale: Targets the prominence features Hahn (2004) found to affect listeners' comprehension.

activities.title: Intelligibility feedback from diverse listeners
learnerActions: Present a two-minute section to peers from different language backgrounds
Listeners note any moments where they lost track and what caused it
Revise the specific words or stretches identified, rather than the whole accent
activities.intendedInsight: Intelligibility depends on specific, fixable features, not on sounding native.
activities.rationale: Reflects the intelligibility priority argued by Derwing and Munro (2015).

difficulties.pattern: Speaking faster and faster to get through all the content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rising speech rate and fewer pauses as the talk progresses, especially near the end.
difficulties.response: Cut content rather than increasing speed; set time checkpoints. Do not simply tell the speaker to 'slow down' without reducing content.

difficulties.pattern: Distributing stress evenly across words and syllables, so key information does not stand out.
difficulties.revealedBy: Monotone or evenly stressed delivery; listeners miss contrasts and key terms. Speakers whose first languages mark emphasis through word order, particles or syllable timing rather than pitch prominence may transfer these patterns.
difficulties.response: Teach prominence explicitly with contrastive examples from the learner's own talk and practise with recordings.

difficulties.pattern: 'I need to get rid of my accent before I can present.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners focus on individual sounds unrelated to intelligibility, or avoid presenting.
difficulties.response: Discuss the distinction between accent and intelligibility and focus feedback on features that affect understanding.

diagnostic.task: Record the learner delivering one minute of their talk and ask them to mark where they paused and which words they stressed.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Pauses at meaningful boundaries, prominence on key information and a sustainable pace; the learner can describe these choices.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Appropriate pace but even stress, or good prominence with pauses mid-phrase.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Rapid, unpaused delivery or pauses unrelated to meaning.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners focus on thought groups, pace and key-word stress. In-sessional learners refine prominence on technical terms; PGR researchers work on sustaining engaging prosody across longer talks and in large rooms.

guidance.summary: Non-verbal resources such as gaze, gesture, posture and use of space are part of spoken communication and are recognised as paralinguistic features in the CEFR (Council of Europe, 2001). There is little EAP-specific research on teaching non-verbal presentation behaviour, so guidance should be pragmatic and non-prescriptive: help learners use gesture and gaze purposefully, especially to direct attention to visuals, and reduce distracting habits, while respecting individual differences including disability and neurodivergence. Avoid the widely repeated claim that most meaning is conveyed non-verbally, which misapplies experimental findings about conflicting cues to emotion.

activities.title: Sound-off review
learnerActions: Watch a video of yourself presenting with the sound off
Note what supports the message (pointing to visuals, open posture) and what distracts (pacing, fidgeting, back to the audience)
Set one specific goal for the next presentation
activities.intendedInsight: Non-verbal behaviour can be observed and adjusted one feature at a time.
activities.rationale: Video self-review isolates the visual channel that the CEFR identifies as part of communication (Council of Europe, 2001).

activities.title: Point, turn, talk
learnerActions: Practise pointing to a feature on a slide
Turn back to face the audience
Then explain the feature, repeating the sequence for several slides
activities.intendedInsight: Speakers can direct attention to visuals without speaking to the screen.
activities.rationale: Supports the coordination of speech and visuals that research presentations require.

difficulties.pattern: Reading from the screen with the back to the audience.
difficulties.revealedBy: Little audience gaze; the speaker faces the projection.
difficulties.response: Use speaker notes or a confidence monitor and practise the point–turn–talk sequence.

difficulties.pattern: Copying a single 'confident' model of body language that feels unnatural or conflicts with the speaker's own norms or needs.
difficulties.revealedBy: Exaggerated, rehearsed gestures; discomfort; forced sustained eye contact.
difficulties.response: Focus on purposeful, non-distracting behaviour rather than conformity; allow alternatives to sustained eye contact (e.g. scanning, looking between faces) and discuss variation in norms.

diagnostic.task: Watch a two-minute video of the learner with the sound off and ask them to evaluate it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies specific supporting and distracting behaviours and sets a realistic goal.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies general impressions ('I look nervous') without specific behaviours.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify any features or focuses only on appearance.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit most from basic awareness and video review. In-sessional learners adapt to larger rooms, group formats and online cameras.
reviewNotes: Evidence on non-verbal training for L2 academic presenters is thin; these recommendations are practitioner-based.
The often-quoted '7%–38%–55%' figures derive from experiments on inconsistent cues about feelings and should not be applied to presentations.

guidance.summary: Written language is lexically dense, whereas speech spreads information across more clauses (Halliday, 1989), and corpus research shows that spoken university registers differ systematically from academic writing (Biber, 2006). A written script read aloud is therefore hard for listeners to process and is usually delivered with flat prosody. Teach a graduated move from script to prompts, keeping short scripted segments for high-risk moments such as the opening and key definitions.

activities.title: Script-to-prompts ladder
learnerActions: Write a full script for one section of your talk
Highlight the key words, numbers and transitions, then copy only these onto a cue card
Deliver from the cue card, record it, and compare the recording with the script
activities.intendedInsight: Speaking from prompts produces more listenable language than reading a script.
activities.rationale: Makes the difference between written and spoken packaging (Halliday, 1989) audible to the learner.

activities.title: Written sentence, spoken sentence
learnerActions: Take three dense written sentences from your script
Rewrite each as two or three shorter spoken sentences
Say both versions aloud to a partner and ask which is easier to follow
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken academic language unpacks information into clauses.
activities.rationale: Draws on Biber's (2006) evidence of systematic differences between spoken and written university registers.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I don't read, I'll make grammar mistakes or forget something.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Refusal to give up the script; anxiety when notes are reduced.
difficulties.response: Allow scripted openings, definitions and transitions while the rest is delivered from prompts; reduce support gradually. Do not remove all notes at once.

difficulties.pattern: Memorising the whole script word for word.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unnatural rhythm, little eye contact and breakdown if interrupted or a word is forgotten.
difficulties.response: Rehearse from prompts with deliberate variation in wording, and practise recovering from a lost place.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show their notes for a forthcoming presentation and deliver one minute from them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Key-word notes; delivery uses spoken-style sentences with frequent eye contact.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Bullet-point notes that are full sentences, or near-verbatim recall.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A full script read aloud.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners often begin with scripts; the move to prompts should be staged. In-sessional and PGT learners apply the same principles to recorded and online presentations, where reading from screen is tempting.

guidance.summary: Wulff, Swales and Keller (2009) analysed the discussion sessions following talks at a specialised conference and describe them as a distinctive part-genre in which audience turns include comments and suggestions as well as questions. Morita (2000) shows that handling questions in classroom presentations is part of being socialised into a disciplinary community. Teach a listen–clarify–answer–check routine, strategies for critical questions and comments, and honest acknowledgement of limits.

activities.title: Question-type practice
learnerActions: Prepare for four turn types: clarification, challenge to evidence, out-of-scope question and comment or suggestion
Plan a response strategy for each (answer, acknowledge and defend, defer, thank and engage)
Practise in a simulated Q&A with peers playing each role
activities.intendedInsight: Not all Q&A turns are questions, and each type calls for a different response.
activities.rationale: Based on Wulff et al.'s (2009) description of the range of audience turns in discussion sessions.

activities.title: Reformulate before answering
learnerActions: A partner asks a long, multi-part question
The presenter reformulates it briefly and confirms
The presenter answers each part concisely and checks whether the question was answered
activities.intendedInsight: Reformulating buys thinking time and avoids answering the wrong question.
activities.rationale: Builds the interactive competence Morita (2000) describes as part of oral academic socialisation.

difficulties.pattern: Answering immediately, before fully understanding the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that address a different question from the one asked.
difficulties.response: Make reformulation or confirmation a routine first step and allow a short pause.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a critical question as a personal attack.
difficulties.revealedBy: Defensive tone, over-long justification or withdrawal.
difficulties.response: Reframe critical questions as engagement; practise acknowledging the point before responding. Prepare answers to likely challenges in advance.

difficulties.pattern: Not knowing how to say 'I don't know' without losing face.
difficulties.revealedBy: Guessing, evasion or a bare 'I don't know'.
difficulties.response: Teach hedged acknowledgements and offers to follow up, and show that experts use them.

diagnostic.task: After a short presentation, ask a clarification question, a challenge and an out-of-scope question.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reformulates where needed, answers concisely, defends or concedes appropriately and acknowledges limits honestly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Answers relevantly but at length, or becomes defensive under challenge.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Misunderstands questions or cannot respond to the challenge.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners practise in assessed presentations with timed Q&A. In-sessional UG and PGT learners face module Q&A and project panels. PGR researchers handle conference discussion sessions, upgrade panels and vivas, where questions may be expert and searching.

guidance.summary: Leki (2001) found that multilingual undergraduates in group projects were often positioned as less competent and allocated marginal roles, with little guidance from instructors on how groups should work. Group presentations therefore combine language and collaboration demands. Teach shared planning of message and structure, handovers that link content, consistent slides and shared Q&A, using joint rehearsal to integrate the talk; the Companion Volume's goal-oriented co-operation scale describes the language of this kind of joint planning (Council of Europe, 2020).

activities.title: One-sentence message test
learnerActions: Before dividing sections, the group writes the presentation's overall message in one sentence
Each member checks that their section supports that sentence
At the run-through, each member states the message from memory and the group resolves any differences
activities.intendedInsight: A group talk needs one message, not several.
activities.rationale: Makes shared planning concrete and exposes divided planning early.

activities.title: Handover rewriting
learnerActions: Collect the group's handovers from a rehearsal (e.g. 'Now X will talk about…')
Rewrite each to summarise the outgoing section and preview the incoming point
Rehearse the transitions only, several times
activities.intendedInsight: Handovers are signposts that connect content across speakers.
activities.rationale: Applies signposting to the multi-speaker format, where cohesion is most at risk.

difficulties.pattern: Dividing the talk by person rather than by content, so each member prepares a separate mini-presentation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated introductions, inconsistent slides and different messages across sections.
difficulties.response: Require a shared plan and a single slide deck before individual preparation begins.

difficulties.pattern: Multilingual members allocated only slide-making or the shortest speaking part on the basis of assumed language ability.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unequal speaking time; members report being sidelined.
difficulties.response: Address the whole group's assumptions, allocate by content and development goals, and provide support for all speakers.

difficulties.pattern: Handovers limited to names.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abrupt transitions; the audience loses the thread between speakers.
difficulties.response: Practise content-linking handovers and rehearse transitions separately.

diagnostic.task: Ask each group member separately to state the presentation's overall message and how their section contributes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Consistent messages and clear links between sections.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Similar topic descriptions but no shared message.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Members describe unrelated sections.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional programmes often use group presentations as early assessment. In-sessional UG and PGT modules use them widely, often with peer assessment of contribution.

guidance.summary: MacIntosh-Murray (2007) studied poster presentations at a health-services conference and found tensions between the forms of posters, the norms of poster sessions and the value participants attached to them, with presenter–visitor interaction central to their communicative work. Posters are read along visual paths shaped by layout and salience (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006). Teach a short adaptable overview, gauging the visitor, guiding them around the poster and sustaining a conversation.

activities.title: Thirty seconds or two minutes
learnerActions: Prepare a 30-second and a 2-minute overview of your poster
Practise both with a partner who signals how much time they have
Identify which parts of the poster each version points to
activities.intendedInsight: Poster presenters adapt the length of their overview to the visitor.
activities.rationale: Reflects the interactive, visitor-driven nature of poster sessions described by MacIntosh-Murray (2007).

activities.title: Visitor role cards
learnerActions: Visitors receive role cards (specialist, student from another field, potential collaborator, sceptic)
Presenters gauge the visitor with an opening question and adapt their explanation
Visitors give feedback on how well the explanation fitted them
activities.intendedInsight: Poster conversations are dialogues tailored to each visitor.
activities.rationale: Practises the presenter–visitor interaction central to the genre (MacIntosh-Murray, 2007).

difficulties.pattern: Delivering the same memorised monologue to every visitor.
difficulties.revealedBy: Visitors disengage; no questions are invited.
difficulties.response: Practise opening with a question to the visitor and adapting depth; rehearse with varied visitor roles.

difficulties.pattern: Standing silently and waiting for visitors to read the poster.
difficulties.revealedBy: Visitors pass by; few conversations begin.
difficulties.response: Prepare a friendly opening line and a one-sentence summary to offer.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to present their poster to you twice, once as a specialist and once as a non-specialist.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Different explanations adapted to each visitor, using the poster to guide attention.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some adaptation of vocabulary but the same structure and length.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Identical monologue both times.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and UG programmes sometimes use posters as assessed projects. PGT and PGR learners present at departmental events and conferences, where posters are a common entry point to research communities.
reviewNotes: MacIntosh-Murray (2007) is a single case study of one conference; generalisations should be cautious.

guidance.summary: Conference presentations are a key research genre: their introductions combine context, argument and audience interaction (Rowley-Jolivet & Carter-Thomas, 2005), visuals carry much of the argument (Rowley-Jolivet, 2002), and discussion sessions form a distinct part-genre (Wulff et al., 2009). Aguilar (2004) describes the peer seminar as a spoken research process genre in which work in progress is presented to colleagues. Teach researchers to select a take-home message, frame the niche and contribution early, design visuals for the argument and keep strictly to time.

activities.title: Take-home message first
learnerActions: Write the one sentence you want the audience to remember
Design the talk backwards, keeping only content that supports that sentence
Check that the introduction frames the niche and the conclusion restates the message
activities.intendedInsight: A research talk is an argument for one contribution, not a summary of a thesis.
activities.rationale: Applies the argumentative dimension of conference introductions described by Rowley-Jolivet and Carter-Thomas (2005).

activities.title: Comparing research talk formats
learnerActions: Compare a conference talk and a work-in-progress peer seminar in your field (recorded or attended)
Note differences in polish, interaction, length and purpose
Plan how your own talk would change between the two formats
activities.intendedInsight: Research presentation formats serve different purposes in the research process.
activities.rationale: Draws on Aguilar's (2004) characterisation of the peer seminar as distinct from the conference presentation.

difficulties.pattern: Presenting the research like a thesis chapter: long background and methods, little on contribution.
difficulties.revealedBy: Contribution appears only in the final minute or not at all.
difficulties.response: Require the niche and contribution within the first three minutes and cut background accordingly.

difficulties.pattern: Overrunning because all results are included.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rushed final slides; the chair has to intervene.
difficulties.response: Select results for the take-home message and rehearse with strict timing; prepare backup slides for questions.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the discussion session as an examination to survive rather than a dialogue about the research.
difficulties.revealedBy: Defensive or minimal answers; missed opportunities to engage with suggestions.
difficulties.response: Discuss the range of turns in discussion sessions (Wulff et al., 2009) and practise responding to comments and suggestions as well as questions.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to present the first three minutes and last minute of a research talk, then take two questions.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Niche and contribution clear early, a focused take-home message and dialogic answers.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Clear content but contribution emerges late, or answers are defensive.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Background-heavy with no clear contribution; overruns.

guidance.contextNotes: PGT learners present dissertation projects or proposals. PGR researchers present at progression reviews, departmental seminars and conferences, where time limits are strict and audiences are specialist; disciplinary conventions (e.g. results-heavy sciences, text-heavy humanities papers read aloud) vary and should be observed locally.
reviewNotes: In some humanities fields conference papers are traditionally read from a script; guidance on speaking from notes should be adapted to local disciplinary norms.

guidance.summary: Recorded and online presentations are now common in assessment, including on pre-sessional programmes. They remove live audience feedback and allow re-recording, which can encourage reading from a script; learners need the same spoken-style principles as for live talks (Halliday, 1989), plus technical and accessibility skills such as providing accurate captions (W3C, 2023). Assessment rules on editing, length and tool use must be read carefully.

activities.title: Two-take comparison
learnerActions: Record a two-minute section reading from a full script
Record the same section from key-word prompts
Compare the two recordings for naturalness, pace and engagement with peers
activities.intendedInsight: Recorded talks also sound better when delivered from prompts.
activities.rationale: Applies the difference between written and spoken packaging (Halliday, 1989) to recorded formats.

activities.title: Caption check
learnerActions: Generate automatic captions for your recording
Correct errors, especially technical terms, names and numbers
Note which words were misrecognised and check your pronunciation of them
activities.intendedInsight: Captions improve accessibility and can reveal intelligibility issues.
activities.rationale: Applies captioning requirements for prerecorded media (W3C, 2023).

difficulties.pattern: Re-recording endlessly in pursuit of a perfect take.
difficulties.revealedBy: Many hours spent on short recordings; increasingly stilted delivery.
difficulties.response: Set a limit on takes and focus feedback on intelligibility and structure rather than perfection.

difficulties.pattern: Reading a script visible beside the camera, with eyes off the lens.
difficulties.revealedBy: Eye movement across text; written-style language.
difficulties.response: Use prompts placed near the camera and rehearse from them.

difficulties.pattern: Breaching task rules on editing, length or tools (e.g. AI voice or script generation).
difficulties.revealedBy: Submissions that exceed limits or use prohibited tools.
difficulties.response: Read the assessment brief and AI policy with learners and clarify what editing is allowed.

diagnostic.task: Review a 2-minute recorded presentation section and the learner's note on how it was produced.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Clear audio, synchronised slides, natural delivery, corrected captions and compliance with rules.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Technically sound but read from a script, or captions uncorrected.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Poor audio, script reading and rule breaches.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional programmes, especially online ones, often assess recorded presentations. In-sessional UG and PGT modules use them for flexibility; PGR researchers produce recorded conference talks and three-minute research summaries for online events.
reviewNotes: Little published research addresses recorded EAP presentation assessments; guidance is practitioner-based.

guidance.summary: Speech production involves conceptualising, formulating and articulating (Levelt, 1989); rehearsal moves much of the conceptual and formulation work out of the live moment, freeing attention for the audience. Task-based research reviewed by Skehan (1998) indicates that planning tends to improve fluency. Rehearsal should be aloud, timed and section by section, with content cut in advance.

activities.title: Timed run-through with checkpoints
learnerActions: Set a target time for each section and mark checkpoints in your notes
Rehearse aloud with a timer, recording actual times
Cut or condense sections that overrun and rehearse again
activities.intendedInsight: Timing problems are solved by planning cuts, not by speaking faster.
activities.rationale: Applies findings on planning and fluency (Skehan, 1998) to presentation rehearsal.

activities.title: The emergency version
learnerActions: Prepare a version of your talk that is one third shorter
Decide in advance which sections or slides you would skip
Rehearse switching to the short version mid-talk
activities.intendedInsight: A planned short version protects the key message when time is cut.
activities.rationale: Builds flexibility for real presentation conditions, where sessions often run late.

difficulties.pattern: Rehearsing silently or by reading through the slides.
difficulties.revealedBy: First aloud delivery is in the assessment; large overruns.
difficulties.response: Require evidence of aloud, timed rehearsal (e.g. a recording).

difficulties.pattern: Planning to speak faster if time runs short.
difficulties.revealedBy: No cuts planned; rapid delivery at the end.
difficulties.response: Show that faster speech reduces intelligibility; plan section-level cuts.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what happened in their last rehearsal and what they changed.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reports timed, aloud rehearsals with specific changes and planned cuts.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Rehearsed once without timing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has not rehearsed aloud.

guidance.contextNotes: All stages benefit; foundation and pre-sessional learners need rehearsal built into lessons, while PGR researchers need strict timing for conference slots.
reviewNotes: Skehan (1998) reviews planning studies on L2 tasks rather than presentations; applying them to rehearsal is an inference.

guidance.summary: Seminar expectations are largely tacit and vary by discipline, level, class size and tutor (Ferris & Tagg, 1996), so teaching should make them explicit through observing and analysing real or recorded seminars rather than issuing generic rules. Language socialisation research shows that newcomers learn participation through experience, feedback and negotiation of their position in a group (Duff, 2010; Morita, 2004). Basturkmen's (2003) observation that interaction changed when the tutor joined a student discussion group is a useful prompt for examining how format shapes who speaks and how.

activities.title: Seminar ethnography
learnerActions: Observe a seminar or tutorial in a target discipline (live with permission, or a recording) and note who speaks, how turns are allocated, what kinds of contributions occur and how the tutor responds
Compare notes in groups and draft a 'what counts as a contribution here' list
Check the list against the module handbook or by asking a subject tutor, and revise it
activities.intendedInsight: Participation norms are local and observable, and include questions, tentative ideas and links to readings, not only correct answers.
activities.rationale: Guided observation makes tacit expectations explicit, in line with language socialisation accounts of how newcomers learn participation (Duff, 2010) and with the disciplinary variation Ferris and Tagg (1996) report.

activities.title: Tutor present, tutor absent
learnerActions: Hold two short discussions on the same reading, one with the teacher participating and one without
Compare observer notes or transcripts: who addressed whom, how long turns were, how ideas developed
Decide which features of the student-only discussion to carry into tutor-led seminars
activities.intendedInsight: The presence and moves of a tutor change the interaction; learners can notice and adapt to these patterns.
activities.rationale: Basturkmen (2003) observed different interaction patterns in a student discussion group with and without the tutor; recreating the contrast makes the effect of format visible to learners.

difficulties.pattern: 'The seminar is where the teacher checks we did the reading, so I should only speak when I'm sure I'm right.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners answer tutor questions briefly but never volunteer, ask questions or respond to peers, and describe silence as safer than being wrong.
difficulties.response: Contrast recitation (tutor question, student answer, tutor evaluation) with exploratory discussion using short transcripts, and show tutors valuing tentative and questioning contributions. Present the seminar as a genre with its own rules; do not frame previous educational experience as deficient.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming one tutor's or module's participation norms apply everywhere.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners transfer a style (e.g. frequent interruption, or waiting to be nominated) into a setting where it does not fit, or report confusion when expectations differ.
difficulties.response: Have learners compare two settings and identify the variables (class size, assessment, tutor style, discipline) that shape norms, and encourage them to ask tutors directly about expectations.

difficulties.pattern: Equating participation solely with how much one speaks, and judging oneself or quieter peers as 'not participating'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Self-evaluations focus on talk volume; learners discount listening, note-taking, forum posts or small-group work.
difficulties.response: Discuss Morita's (2004) account of silence as shaped by positioning, power and task conditions, recognise multiple forms of participation, and still build routes into speaking.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'In your next seminar, what do you think the tutor expects you to do before and during the session, and how would you know if you were participating well?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Refers to preparing readings, developing ideas with others, asking questions and the module's criteria, and recognises that expectations vary between tutors.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions reading and speaking but frames contributions as correct answers to the tutor's questions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot describe what happens in a seminar, or treats it as a lecture with occasional questions.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, emphasise the basic distinctions between lectures, seminars and tutorials and why contribution matters. Pre-sessional courses should model the seminar style of the receiving institution and connect it explicitly to any assessed seminar. In-sessional UG and PGT support works best embedded with subject staff, using real module expectations; PGT students on one-year programmes may need this in the first week.
reviewNotes: Ferris and Tagg (1996) surveyed instructors in US institutions; UK and other contexts differ in seminar formats and in whether participation is assessed.

guidance.summary: Preparation is the main lever learners control over the processing load of real-time discussion: task-based research reviewed by Skehan (1998) indicates that pre-task planning tends to benefit fluency and complexity. Morita (2000) describes multilingual graduate students investing heavily in preparation for oral academic activities. Teach preparation as reading for a discussion purpose — recording positions, links and questions with locators — rather than as summarising or scripting.

activities.title: Three-column seminar preparation sheet
learnerActions: For each set reading, record the author's key claim with a page number, a point you agree or disagree with and why, and one question
Add one link between two readings, or between the reading and a previous session
Use the sheet to make a first contribution within the opening ten minutes of the seminar
activities.intendedInsight: Preparation should produce contributions, not only comprehension.
activities.rationale: Structuring preparation around positions and questions shifts planning from comprehension to formulating contributions, the kind of planning that the studies reviewed by Skehan (1998) associate with more fluent output.

activities.title: Predict the questions
learnerActions: In pairs, predict three questions the tutor might ask from the module outline and the reading
Plan a 30-second note-form response to each
After the seminar, compare the predictions with what was actually discussed
activities.intendedInsight: Anticipating questions eases entry into discussion and reveals which aspects of readings tutors prioritise.
activities.rationale: Rehearsing likely responses in note form balances preparedness with the spontaneity seminars require, and the post-seminar comparison builds knowledge of the genre, echoing the preparation practices Morita (2000) describes.

difficulties.pattern: 'I read every word of the article twice, but in the seminar I had nothing to say.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Extensive highlighting or summary notes but no recorded positions or questions; the learner speaks only when asked directly.
difficulties.response: Model preparation for discussion by sharing an expert's notes containing claims, reactions and questions, and set preparation tasks that require a position. Do not respond by assigning more reading.

difficulties.pattern: Writing a full script and reading it aloud when invited to speak.
difficulties.revealedBy: Contributions are long, written in style and disconnected from what was just said; the learner loses their place if interrupted.
difficulties.response: Accept a scripted first contribution as a bridge, then reduce notes to key words and practise adapting a prepared point to link to the previous speaker. Do not ban notes outright, which can raise anxiety.

difficulties.pattern: Underestimating reading time, so preparation covers only the first part of longer texts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes stop part-way through; the learner avoids discussing later sections.
difficulties.response: Teach selective reading for seminar purposes (abstract, introduction, conclusion and the section most relevant to the questions) and plan reading time across the week.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to talk you through their preparation notes for a forthcoming seminar in two minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notes show claims with page references, at least one evaluative reaction and a question or cross-reading link; the learner can phrase a likely contribution.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate summary notes with no position, link or question.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No notes, highlighted text only, or a full script.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners may need guided reading questions and shorter texts. Pre-sessional learners should prepare from authentic readings with discussion questions. In-sessional UG and PGT learners face heavy reading loads, so selective preparation matters most. PGR researchers preparing for reading groups and lab meetings should connect readings to their own projects.
reviewNotes: The planning studies Skehan (1998) reviews used narrative and decision-making tasks; transfer to seminar preparation is an inference, not a tested finding.

guidance.summary: In student discussions, turns are largely taken by self-selection, and learners who wait to be nominated may rarely speak; Basturkmen (2003) shows that the presence of a tutor alters how turns are distributed. Morita's (2004) case studies show that difficulty entering talk is shaped by the pace of exchanges, how learners are positioned and how others respond, not only by proficiency. Teach recognition of transition points, short floor-claiming and floor-holding moves and recovery strategies, and work with tutors to vary how the floor is distributed.

activities.title: Transition-point spotting
learnerActions: Listen to a recorded seminar extract and mark each change of speaker and what signalled it (a completed point, falling intonation, a pause, a question)
Replay the extract and practise entering at each marked point with a short linking phrase
Discuss which entries felt rushed or late and why
activities.intendedInsight: Turns can be entered at recognisable points without waiting for an invitation.
activities.rationale: Explicit noticing of transition cues supports the coordination of listening and speaking that self-selected turn-taking requires.

activities.title: Holding the floor collegially
learnerActions: In groups of four, each person makes a 40-second point while the others try to come in politely
The speaker holds the floor by announcing structure ('two things here…'), using fillers or asking to finish
Swap roles and discuss where floor-holding becomes domination
activities.intendedInsight: Holding a turn while formulating is legitimate and can be done collegially.
activities.rationale: Gives learners rehearsed resources for the moments when they need formulation time, reducing the risk of losing the turn mid-idea; students in Ferris (1998) reported whole-class discussion as particularly demanding.

difficulties.pattern: 'I wait for a long enough pause to be polite, but by the time I'm ready the topic has moved on.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Late or abandoned entry attempts; prepared ideas are never voiced.
difficulties.response: Teach short floor-claiming moves that buy formulation time ('Can I come in on that?', 'Just on that point…') and encourage an early first contribution. Also adjust task design (think time, rounds). Do not simply tell learners to 'be more confident'.

difficulties.pattern: Applying one rule about interruption across all settings — never interrupting, or cutting in frequently to show engagement.
difficulties.revealedBy: No overlapping entries even in fast student-led discussion, or frequent cut-ins that peers find abrupt.
difficulties.response: Compare examples of supportive overlap and competitive interruption, discuss how acceptability depends on group, tutor and topic, and practise mitigated entry.

difficulties.pattern: Entry attempts are ignored or talked over because the learner has been positioned as less competent.
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner reports trying to speak and being overlooked; observation shows peers not taking up their points.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a group dynamic, not only the learner's problem: use structures such as rounds and nomination, and teach all students to take up others' points. Give the learner re-entry moves ('As I was starting to say…').

diagnostic.task: After a 10-minute recorded group discussion, ask the learner to identify one point where they entered and one where they wanted to but did not, and explain what happened.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Self-selects at transition points with linking moves, can name the cues used and recovers from overlaps.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Enters mainly when invited; recognises missed chances but lacks moves to take them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Little or no participation and cannot identify where entry would have been possible.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional classes can begin with structured turn allocation before moving to free discussion. In-sessional UG learners often meet fast discussions among peers who share local references. PGT and PGR settings may include tutor-dominated or strongly argumentative styles, so the emphasis shifts to entering and holding the floor under pressure.
reviewNotes: The notion of transition-relevance places comes from conversation analysis; no listed reference covers it directly.

guidance.summary: Learners often have views but present them as summaries of readings or as unsupported assertions. A short claim–reason–support move, with explicit stance marking, gives a reliable unit for contribution, and framing argument as reasoned position-taking (Andrews, 2010) helps learners see why summary alone is not enough. Basturkmen (2002) shows that ideas in seminars are elaborated across several turns, so learners also need to extend their reasoning when asked 'why?' rather than treating the first statement as complete.

activities.title: Claim, reason, support in 45 seconds
learnerActions: Given a discussion question, note a one-sentence position, one reason and one example or source
Deliver it to a partner in 45 seconds
The partner asks 'Why?' or 'What's the evidence?', and the speaker extends with a further reason or a qualification
activities.intendedInsight: A position needs reasons and can be developed further under questioning.
activities.rationale: Makes the basic argumentative unit explicit and rehearses the elaboration across turns that Basturkmen (2002) found in seminar discussion.

activities.title: Summary or view?
learnerActions: Listen to six short, teacher-recorded seminar contributions and classify each as summary, unsupported opinion or supported view
Rewrite two of the weaker ones as supported views
Deliver the rewritten versions and compare them with the originals
activities.intendedInsight: Summary alone is not a contribution, and assertion alone is not persuasive.
activities.rationale: Contrasting examples sharpens learners' sense of what tutors value in discussion.

difficulties.pattern: 'I'll just tell them what the article said — the author is the expert, so my opinion doesn't matter.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Contributions summarise readings without evaluation; the learner hesitates when asked what they think.
difficulties.response: Show that evaluative engagement with readings is expected, model contributions that take a position on a source, and make 'my view is… because…' a required element of practice tasks.

difficulties.pattern: Giving a view with no reasons ('I think it's a good idea').
difficulties.revealedBy: Short assertions; the learner repeats the claim when asked why.
difficulties.response: Require a reason in every practice contribution and work on extension with because, since and for example. Do not prioritise more sophisticated stance phrases before the reasoning is present.

diagnostic.task: Pose a contestable question about a recent reading, allow one minute's thought, ask for the learner's view, then ask 'Why?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: A clear position with a reason and support, extended with a new reason or qualification when challenged.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A position with a vague reason; the claim is restated when challenged.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A summary of the reading with no position.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on clear claim–reason structures on accessible topics. Pre-sessional learners should base views on set readings and data. In-sessional UG learners work on the forms of evidence their disciplines accept for a view.

guidance.summary: Teaching materials often present agreeing and disagreeing as lists of interchangeable phrases, but Basturkmen (2002) shows that in seminar discussion disagreement emerges over several turns as ideas are negotiated. Politeness theory explains why disagreement is usually mitigated (Brown & Levinson, 1987), and research on pragmatic development indicates that explicit attention to pragmatic strategies can support learners (Kasper & Rose, 2002). Teach an acknowledge–locate–reason pattern, calibrated to relationship and stakes, and practise sustaining a disagreement over more than one turn.

activities.title: Disagreement continuum
learnerActions: Rank eight teacher-written responses to a claim from most to least direct
Discuss which would suit a peer, a tutor and a published author, and why
Respond to three new claims at an assigned point on the continuum
activities.intendedInsight: Mitigation is a set of choices adjusted to relationships and stakes, not a fixed formula.
activities.rationale: Explicit metapragmatic discussion is among the instructional approaches Kasper and Rose (2002) review, and the ranking draws on the face concepts of Brown and Levinson (1987).

activities.title: Negotiating over several turns
learnerActions: Read a transcript extract in which a disagreement develops over several turns
Identify where the point of difference becomes clear and how each speaker qualifies their position
Role-play a continuation that reaches a partly shared position
activities.intendedInsight: Disagreement in seminars is a process of negotiating meaning, not a single move.
activities.rationale: Reflects Basturkmen's (2002) analysis of ideas being negotiated across extended exchanges.

difficulties.pattern: 'Disagreeing with the tutor would be disrespectful.'
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner agrees with tutors and authors regardless of their own view, and voices disagreement only privately.
difficulties.response: Show tutors explicitly inviting challenge and examples of respectful disagreement with authority; sequence practice from published authors to peers to tutors. Take the concern seriously rather than dismissing it.

difficulties.pattern: Stacking hedges until the position disappears ('Maybe, perhaps, I'm not sure, but possibly…').
difficulties.revealedBy: Listeners cannot say whether the learner agrees or disagrees.
difficulties.response: Teach one-mitigator-plus-clear-point patterns and have listeners paraphrase the speaker's position as a check.

difficulties.pattern: Bald disagreement ('No, that's wrong') that peers hear as aggressive.
difficulties.revealedBy: Peers respond defensively and the learner is surprised by the reaction.
difficulties.response: Introduce acknowledgement and partial agreement as resources and practise reformulating direct responses. Avoid treating directness as a fault in itself; it can be appropriate in debate or among close peers.

diagnostic.task: Read aloud a claim a peer might make about a recent reading and ask the learner to respond, partly disagreeing.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Acknowledges the claim, locates the specific difference, gives a reason and uses proportionate mitigation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mitigated but vague about the point of difference, or clear but bald.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Agrees by default, or says 'I disagree' with no reason.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need a small set of reliable patterns. Pre-sessional learners should practise disagreeing with readings and tutors. In-sessional UG and PGT learners calibrate to their own tutors and peers. PGR researchers need to disagree with senior academics in research seminars with appropriate authority.

guidance.summary: Seminar talk is co-constructed: Basturkmen (2002) shows ideas developing across several speakers' turns, and Basturkmen (2003) observed more of this collaborative development among students when the tutor was absent. Teach an explicit back-reference plus a stated relation (extend, qualify, contrast, connect), and assess listening as part of speaking.

activities.title: Link-and-add chain
learnerActions: One student makes a point about a reading
Each subsequent speaker names the previous speaker, reformulates their point in a clause and states whether they are extending, qualifying or contrasting it
An observer records the relation used and flags any turn that does not link
activities.intendedInsight: Strong contributions are tied to what has just been said.
activities.rationale: Forces attention to prior turns and makes visible the co-construction of ideas described by Basturkmen (2002).

activities.title: Mapping a discussion
learnerActions: Map a seminar transcript as a diagram showing which turns build on which
Identify turns that start new threads without linking and discuss their effect
Plan two contributions that could have connected separate threads
activities.intendedInsight: Discussion has a structure that participants create through linking moves.
activities.rationale: Visualising exchange structure supports noticing of collaborative development, which Basturkmen (2003) found varied with the participation framework.

difficulties.pattern: 'I prepared three points, so I'll make them whenever I get a chance.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Contributions do not connect to the preceding talk and peers do not take them up.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to adapt a prepared point by first linking it to the current thread; keep preparation but require the link. Do not discourage preparation itself.

difficulties.pattern: Using generic linking openers ('Following on from that…') without engaging the content of the previous point.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic openings followed by unrelated points.
difficulties.response: Require a reformulation of the previous point before the new one and give feedback on its accuracy.

diagnostic.task: Play a 1-minute recorded seminar turn and ask the learner to respond by building on it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurately reformulates the point, states a relation and adds something new.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Links generically and adds content only loosely related to the turn.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Makes an unrelated point or simply agrees.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional programmes should introduce linking as a core discussion skill. In-sessional UG and PGT learners need it in fast discussions where peers share background knowledge, and PGT seminar criteria often reward synthesis of peers' contributions. In PGR reading groups, building on others includes relating colleagues' points to different research projects.

guidance.summary: Subject instructors surveyed by Ferris and Tagg (1996) identified asking and answering questions and taking part in discussion as areas of difficulty for multilingual students, and students in Ferris (1998) reported class discussion as demanding. Questions are both a comprehension-repair strategy and a legitimate contribution that can move a discussion on (Basturkmen, 2002). Teach targeted questions that pinpoint the problem, form-focused work on direct and embedded questions, and mitigation proportionate to the relationship.

activities.title: Pinpoint the problem
learnerActions: Listen to a short lecture or seminar extract containing an unclear term and an unsupported claim
Write a question that names exactly what is unclear or unsupported
Compare the answers a pinpointed question and 'Can you repeat?' would receive
activities.intendedInsight: Specific questions get specific help and show engagement.
activities.rationale: Linking questions to comprehension monitoring supports listening as well as speaking, addressing a difficulty instructors reported in Ferris and Tagg (1996).

activities.title: Question types for discussion
learnerActions: Sort sample questions into clarification, elaboration, evidence, implication and connection types
Write one question of each type about a set reading
Use them in a seminar and note which ones generated further discussion
activities.intendedInsight: Different questions do different work in a discussion.
activities.rationale: Extends questioning beyond repair to the idea-developing exchanges observed in seminar discussion (Basturkmen, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: 'Asking a question shows everyone that I didn't understand.'
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner never asks in class but asks peers or approaches the tutor afterwards.
difficulties.response: Normalise questions by modelling expert questions and asking tutors to invite them; start with written or small-group questions. Do not require public questions before safer routes have been established.

difficulties.pattern: Retaining question word order in embedded questions ('Could you tell me what does this mean?').
difficulties.revealedBy: Inverted order in indirect questions, especially when the learner is mitigating.
difficulties.response: Give brief focused practice on embedded question order, but in live discussion prioritise getting the question asked over accuracy.

difficulties.pattern: Prefacing questions to tutors with so much apology that the question is lost.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long apologetic prefaces; the tutor has to ask what the question is.
difficulties.response: Practise one mitigator followed by a direct question, and discuss evidence that tutors generally welcome clear questions.

diagnostic.task: Play a 2-minute talk extract and ask the learner to put one question about something unclear and one about something they want to know more about.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Both questions pinpoint content, are intelligible and appropriately mitigated.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A generic clarification request, or form problems that obscure the question.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No question, or only 'I don't understand.'

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need question forms and routines. In-sessional learners focus on asking in large classes and lectures as well as seminars. PGR researchers ask questions after research talks, where questions also position the asker within the field.
reviewNotes: Ferris and Tagg (1996) and Ferris (1998) report US data; the reported difficulty with questions should not be generalised to all multilingual students.

guidance.summary: In multilingual academic groups mutual understanding cannot be assumed, because members differ in accent, proficiency and disciplinary background. Research on English as a lingua franca in international universities frames communicative success as achieved through accommodation and negotiation rather than conformity to native-speaker norms (Jenkins, 2014), and Basturkmen (2002) shows seminar meaning being negotiated across turns. Teach confirmation checks, paraphrase-back and self-reformulation as normal collaborative moves.

activities.title: Paraphrase-back pairs
learnerActions: Speaker A explains a concept from their reading in one minute
Speaker B paraphrases it back and asks for confirmation
A confirms or reformulates with an example; then the pair swaps roles
activities.intendedInsight: Checking is efficient and collaborative, not an admission of failure.
activities.rationale: Practises the negotiation of meaning that supports mutual intelligibility in multilingual groups (Jenkins, 2014).

activities.title: Rescue the explanation
learnerActions: Explain a technical term from your field to a partner from a different field
The partner signals non-understanding whenever a term or step is unclear
Reformulate with a simpler term, an example or an analogy until the partner can paraphrase it
activities.intendedInsight: Reformulation is a skill speakers can plan for and practise.
activities.rationale: Builds a repair repertoire for the points at which explanations break down in cross-disciplinary groups.

difficulties.pattern: Nodding as if understanding to avoid interrupting.
difficulties.revealedBy: Apparent agreement followed by responses that miss the point.
difficulties.response: Model checks as routine in teacher talk, and reward accurate paraphrase rather than speed in tasks.

difficulties.pattern: Repeating the same words more loudly or slowly when not understood.
difficulties.revealedBy: Identical wording repeated; the listener remains confused.
difficulties.response: Teach explicit reformulation strategies (a simpler synonym, an example, breaking the idea into steps).

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain a concept to a partner who has been told to misunderstand once.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notices the misunderstanding, reformulates with new wording or an example, and checks again.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices but repeats the original wording.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not notice the misunderstanding.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners practise basic checks and paraphrase. In-sessional UG and PGT learners use them in diverse groups and when explaining disciplinary terms to peers from other fields, where all students — including home students — benefit from the same practices.

guidance.summary: Seminar tutors expect discussion to engage with set readings; Morita (2000) describes graduate students' presentations and discussions in which critical engagement with assigned texts was central. Oral attribution adapts written signal phrases to speech: a brief reference to the author or text, the point, and the speaker's comment, sometimes with a page reference to direct peers. As in writing, attribution also positions the speaker in relation to the literature (Hyland, 1999).

activities.title: Source, point, comment
learnerActions: Prepare three cards, each with an author, a key point and a page number
In discussion, use each card once: state the source, paraphrase the point and add your own comment
Observers note whether the boundary between source and comment was audible
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken attribution is brief but makes clear whose idea is whose.
