activities.rationale: Transfers the attribution and positioning functions of written citation (Hyland, 1999) to speech.

activities.title: Quote or paraphrase?
learnerActions: Compare a contribution that reads a long quotation aloud with one that paraphrases briefly and gives the page
Discuss which is easier to follow and which shows the speaker's view
Rework a quotation-based contribution into a brief paraphrase with a locator and comment
activities.intendedInsight: Reading long quotations aloud slows discussion and hides the speaker's own view.
activities.rationale: Listeners hear speech once, so brevity and explicit stance help discussion move.

difficulties.pattern: Presenting points from readings as if they were the learner's own knowledge.
difficulties.revealedBy: Tutor or peers ask 'Where is that from?'
difficulties.response: Make attribution a required element of practice contributions and connect it explicitly to written attribution practices.

difficulties.pattern: Reading long passages aloud from the text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Contributions consist of extended quotation with no comment.
difficulties.response: Limit quotation to a short phrase and require a comment after every source reference; prepare paraphrases in advance.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to make a 1-minute contribution that uses one set reading to support or challenge a peer's point.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Clear attribution, a brief and accurate paraphrase and an explicit comment.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Attribution present but no comment, or reliance on a long quotation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No attribution.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners practise with set readings. In-sessional UG and PGT learners use module readings and disciplinary conventions for referring to authors, cases, statutes or datasets in speech. PGR researchers refer to literature in reading groups and when positioning their own work.
reviewNotes: Research on oral attribution in student seminars is limited; this guidance extrapolates from written source-use research and studies of graduate oral activities.

guidance.summary: Student-led seminars often assess facilitation, and the CEFR Companion Volume treats facilitating collaborative interaction and managing interaction as mediation competences (Council of Europe, 2020). Morita (2000) describes graduate students leading class discussion as part of oral academic presentations. Because facilitation requires attending to participation and process, teach it as a set of identifiable moves: opening question, turn distribution, probing, redirection, time-signalling and summarising.

activities.title: Facilitator moves toolkit
learnerActions: Watch a recorded facilitated discussion and label each facilitator move (open, invite, probe, redirect, summarise, close)
Plan a 10-minute discussion with an opening question and three follow-up probes
Facilitate the discussion and receive observer feedback on the moves used
activities.intendedInsight: Facilitation consists of identifiable moves that can be planned and practised.
activities.rationale: Breaks a complex mediation skill into observable components, aligned with the Companion Volume's mediation scales (Council of Europe, 2020).

activities.title: Participation map
learnerActions: An observer draws lines between speakers on a seating plan during the first 10 minutes
The facilitator reviews the map at a break
In the next 10 minutes the facilitator uses invitations, rounds or pair-then-share to widen participation
activities.intendedInsight: Facilitators can see and change who participates.
activities.rationale: Makes the effect of facilitation on participation visible, connecting to Basturkmen's (2003) observation that the participation framework shapes interaction.

difficulties.pattern: The facilitator gives their own view after each contribution and becomes the hub of all exchanges.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long facilitator turns; exchanges run only between facilitator and individual participants.
difficulties.response: Limit facilitator content turns and practise probes that hand the floor back. Do not forbid content altogether; brief framing and synthesis are useful.

difficulties.pattern: Working through a list of prepared questions without following up answers.
difficulties.revealedBy: Each question is answered once and the next is asked; ideas are not developed.
difficulties.response: Practise follow-up probes ('Can you say more about…?', 'How does that fit with what X said?') and listening for points to connect.

difficulties.pattern: Putting quieter participants on the spot by nominating them without warning.
difficulties.revealedBy: Nominated participants freeze or give minimal answers.
difficulties.response: Use advance notice, rounds, pair-then-share or written input before nominating.

diagnostic.task: The learner facilitates a 10-minute discussion while an observer maps participation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A clear opening, broad participation, follow-up probes, time management and a fair closing summary.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Questions asked in sequence with little follow-up; some imbalance in participation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The facilitator dominates or the discussion stalls.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and in-sessional UG learners may facilitate assessed student-led seminars. PGT learners often lead discussions of readings. PGR researchers chair reading groups, lab meetings and conference sessions, where time management and fair turn distribution among senior and junior colleagues are central.

guidance.summary: Summarising a discussion requires selecting and generalising across contributions rather than replaying them, a process analogous to the macro-rules identified for summarising written texts (Brown & Day, 1983). The Companion Volume includes note-taking in seminars and meetings among its mediation activities (Council of Europe, 2020). Teach listening for positions and agreements during discussion, structured note grids, and short, thematically organised report-backs.

activities.title: Positions, agreements, open questions
learnerActions: During a discussion, a note-taker uses a three-part grid: positions, points of agreement or disagreement, open questions
After the discussion, the note-taker has two minutes to prepare a 60-second report
The group rates the report for fairness and selectivity
activities.intendedInsight: A summary selects and organises; it does not replay the discussion.
activities.rationale: Applies the summarising operations of deleting, generalising and constructing (Brown & Day, 1983) to spoken discussion.

activities.title: Who said what, or what was said?
learnerActions: Compare a chronological report-back with a thematically organised one on the same discussion
Identify what the thematic version omits and why
Rewrite a chronological report-back thematically
activities.intendedInsight: Thematic organisation communicates the outcome of a discussion more clearly.
activities.rationale: Contrasting models makes the selection criteria for summarising explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Reporting every contribution in the order it was made.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long, list-like report-backs that overrun.
difficulties.response: Impose a time limit and the three-part structure, and practise generalising several contributions into one position.

difficulties.pattern: Presenting one's own view as the group's conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Group members dispute the summary.
difficulties.response: Practise attributing positions and marking disagreement explicitly; have peers check the summary for fairness.

diagnostic.task: After a recorded 10-minute discussion, ask the learner for a 60-second summary.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Selective, thematically organised, fair, and includes an unresolved question.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate but chronological and over-detailed.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Major omissions, or the learner's own view presented as consensus.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and in-sessional UG learners report back from group tasks. PGT learners summarise in assessed seminars. PGR researchers summarise discussions in meetings and reading groups, sometimes as written records.
reviewNotes: Brown and Day (1983) studied summarising written texts; its application to spoken discussion is an analogy.

guidance.summary: Foreign language classroom anxiety involves communication apprehension, test anxiety and fear of negative evaluation (Horwitz et al., 1986), and willingness to communicate is situational, shaped by enduring factors and by the immediate interlocutor, group and topic (MacIntyre et al., 1998). Morita (2004) shows reticence in graduate classrooms shaped by positioning and power relations rather than reducible to culture or personality. Teaching should therefore address both learner strategies and classroom conditions, and should avoid labelling learners as 'quiet students'.

activities.title: Mapping willingness to speak
learnerActions: List recent speaking situations and rate your willingness to speak in each
Identify what made each easier or harder (preparation, group size, topic, tutor moves, peers)
Choose one condition to change and one strategy to try in the next seminar, then review the outcome
activities.intendedInsight: Willingness to speak varies by situation, and some of the conditions can be changed.
activities.rationale: Applies MacIntyre et al.'s (1998) situational model of WTC to learners' own experience to locate actionable factors.

activities.title: Graded entry
learnerActions: Plan an early, low-risk contribution (agreeing with a reason, asking a clarification question)
Make it within the first ten minutes of the seminar
Over several sessions, move to higher-risk contributions such as disagreement or a new idea
activities.intendedInsight: An early, small contribution lowers the barrier to later ones.
activities.rationale: A graded sequence targets fear of negative evaluation (Horwitz et al., 1986) through experiences of success rather than exhortation.

difficulties.pattern: 'I'm just a shy person; I'll never speak in seminars.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Fixed-trait explanations and avoidance of speaking tasks.
difficulties.response: Explore how willingness varied across situations, set small achievable goals and avoid labels. Refer to wellbeing services if anxiety is severe.

difficulties.pattern: Teachers or peers attributing a student's silence to their national or cultural background.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comments such as 'students from X don't participate' in staff or peer talk.
difficulties.response: Discuss evidence that silence reflects positioning, task design and processing load (Morita, 2004), and change discussion design (think time, small groups, rounds) rather than the student's 'culture'.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe one seminar in which they spoke and one in which they did not, and what was different.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies situational factors and strategies they used or could use.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies factors but proposes no strategies.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Attributes the difference entirely to a fixed trait.

guidance.contextNotes: Anxiety may be acute on pre-sessional programmes where progression depends on assessed speaking. In-sessional UG and PGT students may face large classes and peers who share local references. PGR researchers may experience anxiety in research seminars and vivas. Across stages, coordinate with subject staff on discussion design.
reviewNotes: EAP teachers are not counsellors; severe or persistent anxiety should be referred to appropriate support services.

guidance.summary: The CEFR Companion Volume added scales for online interaction, recognising it as a mode with distinct demands (Council of Europe, 2020). In videoconference seminars, reduced gaze and gesture cues and audio delay make turn-taking harder, while chat and reactions provide additional channels; research on videoconferencing in language education highlights the coordination of these multimodal resources (Hampel & Stickler, 2012). Teach explicit bidding, addressing and yielding, purposeful chat use and breakout-room routines.

activities.title: Platform protocol
learnerActions: Agree group conventions for raising hands, using chat and muting
Hold a 10-minute discussion following the protocol
Review a recording to find where turn-taking broke down and revise the protocol
activities.intendedInsight: Online turn-taking works better with explicit, agreed conventions.
activities.rationale: Explicit conventions compensate for the reduced non-verbal cues of online interaction, which the Companion Volume treats as a distinct mode (Council of Europe, 2020).

activities.title: Chat as a second channel
learnerActions: During an online discussion, one member posts sources and questions in the chat
Spoken participants explicitly take up chat contributions
Afterwards, discuss when the chat supported the discussion and when it distracted
activities.intendedInsight: Chat can widen participation when it is integrated with the spoken discussion.
activities.rationale: Draws on the multimodal affordances of videoconferencing described by Hampel and Stickler (2012).

difficulties.pattern: Contributing only through chat to avoid speaking.
difficulties.revealedBy: Many chat messages but no spoken turns.
difficulties.response: Value chat as an entry point, then plan one spoken contribution that develops a chat post.

difficulties.pattern: Talking over others because of audio delay, then both speakers stopping.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated overlaps and false starts in recordings.
difficulties.response: Use explicit addressing and handover phrases and ask a facilitator to allocate turns; confirm before continuing after disruption.

diagnostic.task: Review a recorded online seminar with the learner and ask them to comment on their participation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Appropriate bidding, explicit addressing and yielding, and purposeful chat use.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Participates but with awkward turn-taking or chat that runs separately from the discussion.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Silent, or present only in the chat.

guidance.contextNotes: Relevant at every stage where online or hybrid teaching occurs, including pre-sessional courses delivered online and PGR supervision and research-group meetings with remote collaborators. Hybrid rooms add the challenge of including remote participants in in-room talk.
reviewNotes: Hampel and Stickler (2012) is a proposed reference not yet in the bibliography; check it before publication and remove dependent claims if unverified.
Little research addresses student-led academic seminars online specifically; guidance is partly practitioner-based.

guidance.summary: Debate formats train rapid argument construction, rebuttal and concession under time pressure. Kuhn (1991) found that many people have difficulty generating counter-arguments and rebuttals for their own positions, which suggests these moves need explicit teaching. Andrews (2010) discusses argument in higher education as both exploration and persuasion; learners should recognise that debate rewards adversarial advocacy, which differs from the exploratory norms of most seminars.

activities.title: Strongest objection first
learnerActions: Before the debate, each side lists the three strongest arguments for the opposing side
Prepare a rebuttal or concession for each
In the debate, rebut at least one of the opposition's strongest arguments
activities.intendedInsight: Effective rebuttal targets the opposition's strongest points.
activities.rationale: Addresses the difficulty in generating counter-arguments and rebuttals identified by Kuhn (1991).

activities.title: Debate versus seminar
learnerActions: After a debate, hold a seminar discussion on the same topic
Compare the moves used in each format
Discuss when each mode is appropriate in academic settings
activities.intendedInsight: Adversarial and exploratory argument serve different purposes.
activities.rationale: Makes explicit the distinction between exploratory and persuasive argument discussed by Andrews (2010).

difficulties.pattern: Restating one's own case instead of rebutting the opposition.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rebuttal speeches repeat the constructive speech.
difficulties.response: Require rebuttals to begin by restating the specific opposing point being answered.

difficulties.pattern: Carrying the adversarial debate style into seminars.
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner treats seminar discussion as a contest to win and rarely builds on others.
difficulties.response: Contrast the two modes explicitly and practise switching between them on the same topic.

diagnostic.task: After an opposing speech, ask for a 90-second rebuttal with two minutes' preparation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Targets the strongest opposing point, explains why it fails and concedes where appropriate.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Rebuts a minor point or asserts that the opposition is wrong without explanation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats own case.

guidance.contextNotes: Debate is common on foundation and pre-sessional programmes as a vehicle for oral argument. In-sessional UG use depends on the discipline (e.g. law moots, politics). It is rarely relevant at PGT or PGR level except in specific professional programmes.
reviewNotes: Kuhn's (1991) participants were not EAP learners; the finding is used as a general rationale for explicit teaching of rebuttal.

proposedReferences.apa: Storch, N. (2005). Collaborative writing: Product, process, and students' reflections. *Journal of Second Language Writing, 14*(3), 153–173.
proposedReferences.note: High confidence in authors, year, title and journal; volume, issue and pages believed correct but should be verified. DOI omitted because I am not certain of it. The study compares pairs and individuals writing in an ESL classroom; it is cited only for the general claim that joint writing prompts collaborative attention to ideas and language, not for extended group projects.

authorNotes: grw.inclusive-collaboration overlaps with idn.intercultural-communication, idn.elf and sem.facilitating; it is scoped here as practical group behaviour, with the IDN topics as conceptual prerequisites.

grw.collaborative-writing overlaps with dig.digital-collaboration (tools) and int.collusion (boundaries). I made int.collusion a soft prerequisite; the INT author should not make int.collusion depend on grw.collaborative-writing.

grw.contribution-assessment overlaps with fbk.self-peer-assessment and pub.authorship (contributor roles at PGR level). Consider a PGR-level link from pub.authorship to this topic, or extending scope note to co-authorship contribution statements.

Gap: online and asynchronous group collaboration (time zones, messaging norms in group chats) has no dedicated topic; it is split between grw.meetings, prg.messaging-channels and dig.digital-collaboration.

Gap: there is no topic on group-work assessment design for teachers; the domain is learner-facing, but research such as Leki (2001) implies that inclusive outcomes depend on course design as much as on learner skills.

prs.signposting overlaps heavily with coh.spoken-signposting and lis.lecture-discourse-markers; I treat prs.signposting as the productive, presentation-specific application (including prosodic boundary marking and handovers). Consider whether coh.spoken-signposting should be receptive-and-general only.

prs.slide-design overlaps with mmd.multimodal-literacy, mmd.accessibility and dat.creating-visuals; linked as soft prerequisites. mmd.poster-design is the design counterpart of prs.posters; I have made it a hard prerequisite, so the MMD author should not make mmd.poster-design depend on prs.posters.
prs.handling-questions is likely a prerequisite of pub.viva, exm.oral-exams and dad.studio-critique; those authors should not make prs.handling-questions depend on them.

prs.research-presentations spans conference talks, research seminars and progression/upgrade presentations; consider a separate PGR topic for short-format public research talks (e.g. three-minute thesis-style), which differ in audience and purpose and currently fall between this topic and pub.research-engagement.

Gap: there is no topic on presenting a case or critique in professional-practice formats (e.g. clinical case presentations, design crits), other than dad.studio-critique and dhl.case-reports-care-plans; these could link here.

sem.checking-understanding overlaps with sem.questions-clarification (confirmation checks are a sub-type of clarification) and with prn.repair (self-reformulation). Scoped here as mutual-understanding management in multilingual groups; consider merging or sharpening scope notes.

sem.opinions (LINGUISTIC) and arg.oral-argument overlap. I treat sem.opinions as the basic claim–reason–support turn and arg.oral-argument as more extended real-time argument, so sem.debate depends on arg.oral-argument but sem.opinions does not. The ARG author should avoid making arg.oral-argument a prerequisite of sem.opinions.

sem.speaking-anxiety covers speaking generally (including presentations) but sits in SEM; consider moving it to a cross-cutting place or renaming to make clear it also serves PRS. exm.test-anxiety overlaps for assessed speaking.

Gap: there is no topic for listening-for-participation in large lectures (asking questions in lectures) or for academic small talk/phatic interaction with peers, both of which affect integration and WTC.
Gap: seminar participation as an assessed component (how participation marks are awarded, self-evidencing participation) is not covered; it currently has to be folded into sem.seminar-purposes.
